title: Council Post: Universal Basic Intelligence: The Next Frontier In Societal Welfare
text:
Chairman, Cofounder & Chief AI Officer at Mobeus. Former CTO, CDO & CIO at Fortune 500 Firms in Financial Services and Healthcare.
In the grand arc of human history, a subtle yet profound narrative has been consistently unwinding—the narrative of welfare. From the earliest communal societies to our complex modern-day civilizations, there has been a steady and unmistakable trend: Humans have been progressively taking care of one another's welfare with increasing sophistication and scope.
This narrative is not just a backdrop to our history; it is a cornerstone of our societal evolution—one that reflects our growing recognition of interdependence, compassion and collective responsibility.
Public education and healthcare stand as monumental pillars in this narrative, epitomizing humanity's decision to collectively invest in the well-being of its members. Education has transformed from a privilege of the elite to a fundamental right (universal basic education), ensuring that every child is endowed with the knowledge and skills needed to thrive.
Similarly, public healthcare, or universal basic healthcare, has emerged to much of the world as a societal commitment to protect each individual's health, recognizing it as a precondition for a productive and fulfilling life.
The conversation of collective welfare has evolved to include the concept of universal basic income (UBI). UBI represents a radical rethinking of Social Security, proposing a guaranteed income for all as a cushion against the economic uncertainty wrought by rapid technological change and globalization.
Despite its potential, UBI has been met with considerable resistance, with debates centering on its feasibility, its impact on labor markets and the philosophical implications of "money for nothing." The current state of UBI is fraught with contention and pilot programs, leaving its future uncertain.
Amid these discussions, a new welfare consideration looms on the horizon that's equally as transformative as education and healthcare—the division between the AI-assisted and the unassisted. In this dawning era of AI, the disparity between those who have access to AI and those who do not is poised to become a chasm, dividing society into the "AI-haves" and the "AI-have-nots." The implications of this divide are profound, touching on every aspect of human capability and potential.
For those who can access them, AI assistants will boost people's productivity, give them new and more powerful capabilities, accelerate their learning abilities and help them stay healthy. The AI-haves will boost their knowledge, intuition, creativity, problem-solving and social skills, and they'll have access to powerful AI-based services, including financial advice, career coaching and AI-enhanced healthcare services. Meanwhile, the AI-have-nots will increasingly be left behind.
Enter the concept of universal basic intelligence (UBIQ). UBIQ is not just about the democratization of technology; it's about ensuring that every individual has access to the AI tools that will define the future of work, creativity and daily life. Without UBIQ, we risk exacerbating inequalities and creating a society where a select few hoard the benefits of AI while the rest are left to fend off obsolescence.
How do we bridge this digital divide? There are several paths we might take. One is through taxation—leveraging the wealth that AI generates to increase AI literacy and fund access to AI for all.
Another is the "data dividend" approach, similar to how social media access is funded today, where individuals contribute their data for AI training and, in return, receive AI services—or some different form of a symbiotic exchange where data becomes the currency for intelligence similar to the principles of the 31st Human Right proposed by a collaboration between Hu-manity.co and IBM where human data is classified as human property.
A third avenue could be direct government investment in AI infrastructure and education, ensuring that the AI revolution benefits all rather than just those who can afford it.
However the divide is bridged, the rollout of UBIQ is likely to be as uneven as the technologies that preceded it. Some countries may lead the charge and rapidly integrate AI into their societal frameworks, while others may lag—creating new dynamics in immigration, economic disparity and global competitiveness. As with education and healthcare, we must strive for a world where access to AI is as universal and standardized as access to literacy and medicine.
The digital divide is not a looming challenge of the future but a pressing issue of the present. Approximately 60% of the global population has acquired internet access, granting them immediate entry to the realm of advanced AI, with its myriad of tools and services. This majority now enjoys the considerable advantages conferred by AI, from enhanced learning opportunities to improved productivity.
In stark contrast, the 40% without internet connectivity are excluded from these benefits, resulting in a pronounced and immediate division. This discrepancy is not self-correcting and calls for deliberate and strategic action to bridge the gap.
We must confront this inequality with intentionality and actively work to ensure equitable access to technology, information and AI resources. Without such efforts, the gulf between the connected and AI-assisted and the unconnected and unassisted will only widen, exacerbating existing disparities and hindering collective progress.
One of my favorite quotes from The AI Summit New York 2023 is, "GenAI isn't for some; it's for all." This inclusive perspective was championed by leaders from AI-consuming firms like Deloitte, PwC, Accenture, KPMG, EY and Salesforce throughout the conference. In contrast, there was a noticeable absence of this viewpoint among some major AI-producing entities.
The dialogue around UBIQ should be part of the broader conversation about AI ethics, trustworthy AI and responsible AI. As we architect the AI-infused future, we must ensure the principles of equity, inclusivity and the common good are underpinning it.
Our history shows us that the welfare of each individual strengthens the fabric of society as a whole. The intelligence era should be no different. By embracing UBIQ, we can continue the narrative of welfare that has been central to our shared human story, ensuring that AI becomes a force for collective empowerment, not division.

title: The AI Revolution In Lead Generation:Navigating New Business Frontiers

title: Here’s How AI And Tech Giants Say They’ll Moderate Content In 2024—The World’s Biggest Election Year
text:
Topline
Billions of people are voting in elections across the world this year, which experts fear could be undermined by increasingly popular artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT and the misinformation they enable, prompting some of the world’s biggest tech companies to publicly disclose how they plan to moderate content.
Key Facts
OpenAI, the company behind popular generative AI products including chatbot ChatGPT and image generator Dall-E, has said it will ban politicians, political campaigns and lobbying using its tools and stop applications that might deter people from voting.
Users will also be prohibited from impersonating candidates, officials or governments using the tools and the company said it will introduce authentication tools that will help voters assess whether to trust an image.
Meta, whose family of apps include Facebook, Instagram, Threads and WhatsApp, claims said it will continue longstanding practices in 2024 like labeling state-controlled media, blocking ads from such outlets targeting people in the U.S. and barring new political ads in the final week of the American campaign, as well as requiring advertisers to disclose whether AI or other digital tools were used to create or alter content for political, social and election related advertisements.
Alphabet’s Google, which claims it was the first tech company to require election advertisers to prominently disclose whether content was digitally altered or generated with AI or other tools, said it will limit the types of election-related queries its AI chatbot Bard and other generative AI products can answer.
Video platform Youtube, which is also owned by Alphabet, will require content creators to disclose whether they’ve created realistic synthetic or altered content in 2024, so it can be labeled to tell viewers, a strategy the company said should stave off potential harms from “AI’s powerful new forms of storytelling.”
X, formerly known as Twitter, is regularly criticized for its failure to tackle high levels of falsehoods and misinformation spreading on the platform and last year scrapped tools for reporting election misinformation and fired its election integrity team, which billionaire owner Elon Musk claimed was actually “undermining election integrity.”
The platform promotes its crowdsourced fact-checking scheme Community Notes as the primary means of combating disinformation, a method that has been widely criticized as flawed, error prone and inadequate.
Microsoft said it will offer several services to help protect election integrity, including a tool to help candidates protect their likeness, authenticate content and safeguard both from digital manipulation, supporting and advising campaigns on working with AI and building a hub to support governments in delivering secure elections.
The company also said it will ensure its search engine Bing—whose recently rebranded AI chatbot, Copilot, returned fake and misleading information about recent elections in Europe—gives voters “authoritative” results.
TikTok, owned by Chinese giant ByteDance and largely shunned by politicians despite being a growing source of news, entertainment and debate for younger generations, said it doesn’t allow paid political ads (politicians themselves are allowed) and works with fact-checking organizations to help limit the spread of misinformation.
News Peg
More than half the world’s population are set to go to the polls in 2024 in what has been described as the biggest election year in history. More than 50 countries—including India, the U.S., Britain, Russia, South Africa, Mexico, Indonesia and Pakistan—are slated to hold national elections, and several democracies, including Bangladesh and Taiwan, have already voted. The outcomes of the year’s elections are expected to have significant and global ramifications for the future of democracy and a wide variety of areas including human rights, security and climate action. Not all of these elections are expected to be free and fair and even robust democracies have expressed fears that rising levels of disinformation online and rapidly advancing capabilities of AI tools could undermine the process.
Key Background
AI is ranked as one of the biggest global risks in 2024, largely due to its potential to disrupt elections. Generative AI, which produces content like sound or text from an input prompt, is of particular concern when it comes to ensuring election security over the tools that might be used to convincingly mimic or alter the voice and image of candidates. This year marks the first set of major elections since advanced generative tools were widely adopted by the public, such as image generators Dall-E and Midjourney and chatbots like ChatGPT and Bard. Many big platforms like Facebook and Twitter have been accused of failing to do enough to tackle the spread of misinformation during past elections and fears have grown that the consequences could be far worse now the technology has developed and spread. Deepfakes, fabricated AI content, have been around for some time but recent advances have rendered them both easier to make and more convincing. They have already emerged of Hillary Clinton (implausibly endorsing Ron DeSantis), President Joe Biden (announcing a military draft), former president Donald Trump (getting arrested and running from police). Campaigns are also deploying the technology themselves, such as when Republicans showcased a series of AI-generated images showing what the country would look like if Biden won.

title: Council Post: Two Ways AI Will Help B2B Marketers Beat The Competition In 2024
text:
CEO of Anteriad, a leading provider of B2B marketing solutions. Data-Driven. Tech-Enabled. Growth-Obsessed.
B2B marketers were introduced to many new AI capabilities in 2023. From generative AI like ChatGPT that can help with content to AI algorithms that uncovered new audience segments, 2023 was a year of discovery. Now that B2B marketers have gotten used to the idea that AI will become a major part of their job, it’s time to move past the experimentation phase.
I believe that the B2B marketers who will get out in front of the competition will not only use AI; they will use it more effectively, and in more places, than their peers. Many AI tools are essentially commodities, such as free tools like MidJourney and ChatGPT, and even the AI built into social platforms, customer data platforms (CDPs) and other typical software that B2B marketers use. Other AI capabilities are much more bespoke, tailored to help marketers with specific goals and challenges.
The way to pull ahead is twofold. First, B2B marketers must become more strategic and adept at using these commoditized AI capabilities. Differentiation will come from being better at using the AI that everyone has equal access to.
Second, B2B marketers must embrace custom AI, which can be layered with readily available AI to suit specific business needs or to mine data for unique insights. Using custom AI can unlock hidden potential that can take B2B marketers to the next level in performance.
Mastering The AI Of Today
B2B marketers don’t have to look very far to find AI capabilities that could uncover new insights, save time or optimize performance. A number of platforms in the typical marketing “stack” have released AI capabilities that can amplify current marketing practices, starting with customer data platforms and other companies that house customer data. AI-enabled identity resolution can produce much more complete and accurate customer profiles, while AI-enabled analysis can help produce customer segmentation.
While some B2B marketers have gone through the process of identity resolution and segmentation, few have created a program that is truly fluid. Many B2B marketers allow their data to go stale and their profiles to become outdated. B2B marketers who work with partners to constantly resolve and maintain recent data and to update segments will gain the advantage and get in front of prospects using the most up-to-date insights.
Similarly, B2B marketers who effectively use AI capabilities available through external channels can dramatically improve their overall campaign performance. For example, LinkedIn recently launched a few different AI tools, including one that suggests headlines and copy, while another helps analyze performance. Using these free capabilities regularly will help B2B marketers get the most out of them. Rather than analyze a campaign once and move on, marketers should create a cycle of testing and analyzing that continuously builds on successes to improve more rapidly.
That same concept of testing and learning can also help B2B marketers use ChatGPT, Firefly, MidJourney and other creative AI tools more effectively. Simply asking ChatGPT to write a prospecting email may or may not be better than having a marketer write it. However, asking ChatGPT to write three different emails, testing their performance, and then using those results to go back to the tool and refine the next version will deliver much better results.
Discovering The Power Of Custom AI
The beauty of AI is that it can be layered for even greater effect. B2B marketers can work with partners to build custom AI based on specific needs that can work alongside generally available AI tools. For example, a CDP might have a somewhat limited ability to analyze and segment an audience, while a custom model could bring in data from many more places and deliver more nuanced segmentation.
A custom AI algorithm can also be used to look at both customer profile data and behavior data, such as recent website activity, to understand which customer traits are most valuable. This would help B2B marketers create a better ideal customer profile, prioritize media spend on specific segments, and prioritize sales activity. Custom AI can provide better insight throughout the customer life cycle, uncovering insights like intent to help marketers reach prospects and customers at the right time with the right message.
I’m also a big fan of using AI for a sort of “macro analysis.” While individual tools may have embedded AI capabilities, they have a limited view of the full marketing picture. A custom AI model can look at all the activities and touchpoints across prospects and customers to uncover everything from better cadences to top performing channels, content and offers.
Final Thoughts
The beauty of AI is that it is inherently flexible, and can work with the data that a marketer has today. Of course, AI can be a time saver by automating tasks or generating content or insights quickly, but it should also be thought of as a kind of secret weapon. B2B marketers without centralized data or integrated marketing technology can start to gain advantages even in small ways—for example, analyzing results for a single channel or for current customers, who often have the most complete profiles. Even in this limited capacity, AI can provide value.
While everyone now has access to some level of AI, the marketer who is most thoughtful about where and how to apply it will make the most headway.

title: CUNY Receives Record $75 Million Gift From Simons Foundation
text:
The City University of New York (CUNY), the nation’s largest urban public university system, is being given a $75 million donation from the Simons Foundation, according to an announcement today from New York Governor Kathy Hochul. The gift, the largest in CUNY’s history, will be used to advance computational science and artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives for the system.
One portion of the gift -$25 million – will help underwrite CUNY’s participation in Empire AI – Hochul’s proposal for a consortium of the state’s research universities and other institutions that would form an artificial intelligence computing center in upstate New York.
Plans call for Empire AI to include seven founding institutions—Columbia University, Cornell University, New York University, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, the State University of New York, the City University of New York, and the Simons Foundation.
Hochul intends Empire AI to counter the current concentration of AI resources “in the hands of large technology companies, who maintain outsized control of the AI development ecosystem.” The vision is for Empire AI to make New York a leader in AI research and applications focused on the public interest.
The remaining $50 million from the donation will be used to hire a director for the AI project, add 25 new faculty members and establish a master’s program in computational science at CUNY’s Graduate Center.
CUNY Chancellor Félix V. Matos Rodríguez said, “CUNY is deeply grateful to the Simons Foundation for this historic investment. This generous gift, reflecting our position as a research powerhouse with more than 10,000 researchers and an engine of upward mobility for a student body in which 60% are first-generation college students and more than 80% are persons of color, will propel CUNY to the forefront of research and guarantee access for our diverse community. With this support from the Simons Foundation, CUNY reaffirms its mission to promote educational equity and advance its role as a driver of inclusive growth in New York.”
“For many New Yorkers, higher education is critical to pursuing a career and building a brighter future for themselves,” said Hochul in the release. “This incredible donation from the Simons Foundation will help expand New York’s role in the future of AI at CUNY, preparing our students to fill the jobs of tomorrow right here in our state. With this funding, we are creating more opportunities for our students while solidifying New York as a leader in technology.”
About The Simons Foundation
The Simons Foundation was established by James and Marilyn Simons in 1994. It focuses on support for mathematics, the basic sciences and autism. Jim Simons is the founder of Renaissance Technologies, a quantitative trading hedge fund firm that manages about $50 billion. Forbes recently pegged his wealth at $30.7 billion.
A noted mathematician who earned a BA in mathematics from MIT in 1958 and a PhD in mathematics from the University of California, Berkeley in 1961, Simons served as chair of Stoney Brook University’s mathematics department for a decade. Marilyn Simons earned her bachelor’s degree from Stony Brook in 1974 and her Ph.D. in economics from there in 1984.
Together, the couple’s total philanthropy has been estimated at $4 billion. Last year, the Simons Foundation gave $500 million to Stony Brook University, one of the largest donations to a higher education institution in history.
According to Simons Foundation President David Spergel, the new CUNY gift was inspired by Hochul’s Empire AI proposal. “This gift aims to strengthen computational research at CUNY, to build on its traditions of excellence, its record of inclusion and opportunity, and to enable outstanding students and researchers to have the tools needed to be at the forefront of the field,” said Spergel in the release.

title: Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra Hands-On: AI Is No Longer Just A Buzzword
text:
It was only a matter of time before Samsung put AI at the forefront of its flagship smartphones. While there are some noticeable hardware changes, the Galaxy S24 Ultra is all about AI enhancements to help make lives easier. I wasn’t sold on AI features after using the Google Pixel 8 Pro because they required a lot of time to process. But in my brief time with the Galaxy S24 Ultra ahead of the Galaxy Unpacked 2024, it challenged my outlook towards AI on phones.
Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra goes all-in on AI
The Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra’s AI features aren’t limited to the Gallery app or in photos. Instead, they’re trying to blend into your daily life by being a part of how you use the phone. For instance, the Circle to Search with Google feature allows you to search for anything on the screen with a single tap. You need to press and hold the home button to trigger it and circle an item on the screen with your finger or S Pen.
The object can be anything from a hat on someone’s head to a food item. Once done, Google Search with bring up results for the selected item. It also works with social networking apps like Instagram, so the next time you see an attractive outfit on an influencer, you can use Circle to Search to know more about it.
You could always use the Google app to search for stuff via Google Lens. But the big change here is that it’s not requiring you to take a screenshot, move away from the current screen, and search about the specifics via a separate app. It’s all happening with one press-and-hold. The feature worked flawlessly during the demo, and I see myself using it often in the future.
Samsung is also supercharging its Notes app to deliver a bunch of AI features. You can get a summary of notes that you took during a meeting and translate them. Plus, Samsung Messages app is now capable of translating and displaying messages in your preferred language, and suggesting texts.
The company is going big on translation capabilities with Live Translate, which shows a split screen view on the phone when you are talking to someone who speaks a language you don’t know and vice versa. The feature translates it for the two parties so both of you can understand what is being said by the other person.
Live Translate also works on calls but the process is time-consuming. In the demo, I could speak in Hindi to book a taxi or a reservation. The phone translated it to English for the other side to understand, and whatever was being said from the other side was translated into Hindi for my understanding.
Two things here – first, when using Live Translate during calls, it alerts the call receiver that a translation functionality is being used during the call, which is appreciated. Second, it takes more than two to three seconds to understand, translate, and get the message through to the other side. I’m not sure if the cab driver or the person at the restaurant booking my reservation has that much time and patience to understand and get the work done for me. I’m skeptical about it for now but might change my mind when I review the product.
AI is also coming to Samsung Gallery for more post-editing features like Enhanced Editor that can move subjects, remove reflections, delete objects and fill in the blanks left behind, and add a portrait effect. I snapped a few photos and tried moving objects – with a process similar to Circle to Search. It did so pretty well, faster than the Pixel 8 Pro and I was impressed with the output.
The Galaxy S24 Ultra has a more boxy design
I liked Samsung’s approach with the Galaxy S23 Ultra, where it curved the sides to make the phone more ergonomic. The Galaxy S24 Ultra features the same curved sides but with a flat display. As a result, the phone feels more “boxy” in the hand. It is still big and features a good in-hand feel. I felt like the curvature on the back side has also been reduced, so it feels different from the Galaxy S23 Ultra.
The device features a titanium frame – an upgrade over the Armor Aluminum frame found on the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy S24 Plus. Unlike the iPhone 15 Pro series, the titanium build doesn’t make the Galaxy S24 Ultra considerably lighter but Samsung says it helps with durability.
On the front, you get a 6.8-inch AMOLED display with a Quad HD+ resolution and an adaptive 120Hz refresh rate. It is the same screen as before but with better peak brightness at 2,600 nits. The bezels are slimmer than before but due to the flat screen design, they are now more on-the-face.
It shouldn’t affect the content consumption experience but I prefer curved displays because they make the phones feel slimmer in the hand. However, a flat screen should help with better S Pen input. Talking about the Samsung stylus, it hasn’t changed, so you get the same sensitivity and feedback while using it on the new phone.
Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra adds 5x optical zoom
Samsung has long offered an extra telephoto camera with 10x optical zoom. As a result, zoom ranges between 3x and 10x were not optical quality. But with the Galaxy S24 Ultra, Samsung is going the iPhone 15 Pro Max way. And it is doing so in a better manner because it isn’t skipping 3x.
The Galaxy S24 Ultra replaces its 10MP periscope camera (10x optical zoom) with a 50MP periscope camera that supports 5x optical zoom. Samsung says that photos clicked in 10x will retain similar quality as before due to the better sensor with more megapixels and AI. However, it is technically not optical zoom, and I’m looking forward to test these claims.
As for the numbers, the Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra sports four rear cameras that include a 200MP primary sensor, a 12MP ultrawide-angle lens, a 10MP telephoto camera that supports 3x optical zoom and a 50MP periscope camera with 5x optical zoom. You can still zoom in up to 100x.
Samsung is using its ProVisual AI engine to enhance shots at 1x, 2x, 3x, 5x, and 10x zoom. There’s a new slow-motion video feature in the Gallery that plays a video in slow-mo when you tap and hold on the screen. I liked it, and see myself using it in sports clips.
The Galaxy S24 Ultra also has a new app for more granular camera settings. For example, you can add/remove the zoom shortcuts in the viewfinder, tell the camera that you’re using an anamorphic lens and more.
What else is important?
The Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor in all regions. However, the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy S24 Plus will be powered by the Exynos 2400 chipset in “some regions.” At the time of filing this story, I’m still waiting for clarity from Samsung on that.
The charging wattage remains unchanged on the lineup. This means you get 45W charging on the Galaxy S24 Ultra and Galaxy S24 Plus, while the Galaxy S24 charges at 25W. The trio supports wireless charging but miss out on Qi2 support.
The Galaxy S24 Ultra packs a 5,000mAh battery, while the Galaxy S24 and S24 Plus are getting a 100mAh and 200mAh bump, respectively. I’m yet to test the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3-equipped phone in depth but if it’s as efficient as the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, the battery capacity should be enough.
Another big addition is Samsung promising seven years worth of OS and security upgrades on the Galaxy S24 series.
Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra: Price and availability
You should brace yourself to pay more because the Galaxy S24 Ultra now costs $1,300 for the base 256GB storage option (12GB RAM on all variants) – $100 up from the 1,200 Galaxy S23 Ultra price tag. It’s going close to the OnePlus Open price tag, which offers the novelty of a folding phone. By contrast, the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy S24 Plus will sell at the same $800 and $1,000 mark, respectively.
The Galaxy S24 Ultra will be available in Titanium Black, Titanium Yellow, Titanium Violet, and Titanium Gray color options starting January 31.

title: Company Culture Remains The Competitive Edge In The AI Age
text:
According to a survey by the online education platform edX, 49% of CEOs believe that AI could do their job — perhaps something that many workers would welcome. While we haven’t seen the first AI CEO yet, a recent study led by researchers from University of Oxford predicted that as a result of the accelerating rate of development, AI will beat humans at every possible task by 2047 — 13 years sooner than previously forecasted.
While many are championing the wave of value creation that AI will bring, this exponential speed of change is leaving 77% of people worried about the impact AI will have on society, according to a survey published by Forbes Advisor. That’s causing any sensible leader to wonder what the future workplace will look like, and what they can do to prepare for it. As Donald Rumsfield memorably said, “There are known knowns and known unknowns.”
We know AI will change how people work because take up in knowledge industries is rocketing as workers discover the boost to performance AI can bring. Economists believe AI will also create as many new jobs as are eliminated — at least for now.
We can also be certain that AI won’t change why people work.
People have a complex relationship with paradigm-shifting technologies, lurching between excessive optimism and extreme pessimism. Like the wheel, the printing press, and the internet, the best technologies always disappear and become ordinary. So if it delivers, AI will eventually become a ubiquitous, and almost invisible, workplace tool.
It is impossible for leaders to predict exactly how this disruptive technology will shape the workplace, but as Morgan Housel points out, focusing on what doesn’t change is a successful strategy in uncertain times.
And what really hasn’t changed is people.
For as long as people have existed, we have been driven by three intrinsic motivations: the need for connection, autonomy, and mastery. Fast forward to the modern day, these fundamental aspects of human nature shape our careers and the DNA of organizational life, workplace culture. Countless studies show that when organizations have cultures that engage these motivations, they are rewarded with an increased bottom line and a boost in employee performance. Who creates these cultures? Leaders.
In the age of AI, leaders who can tap into these deep psychological needs and bring people together around shared goals will be rewarded. This was true back when we lived as tribes of hunter-gatherers, and will remain so when AI is woven into every aspect of working life.
“Technologies will come and go, so you need to be able to both ask and answer the question: What do you do as a company, why do you exist?” said Satya Nadella in an interview with Business Insider.
Here are three strategies leaders can use to build great cultures in the AI era:
- Do not outrun our humanity. Recognize that in the race to embrace AI, our intrinsic drives for connection, creation, and learning remain competitive cultural drivers.
- Make AI ordinary. People get anxious in the face of novelty. Remember, we once feared our bodies would disintegrate if we moved as fast as a train ran. Create opportunities to work with and alongside AI to lessen the sense of the strange.
- Augment human capabilities. Remember it’s crucial to integrate AI in a human-centric manner to get the best of the people side of the equation. After all, everything we have ever built, including AI, is the result of human ingenuity.
In a future where access to AI is democratized, an organization’s culture is not just an asset; it's the only moat.

title: Samsung announces new Galaxy S24 lineup with AI-powered photo editing, search features
text:
Samsung announced its new flagship Galaxy S24 smartphone range Wednesday, earlier than expected, touting new artificial intelligence features as the company looks to kick off 2024 with a bang.
As is standard with Samsung's flagship range now, the S24 range comes in three versions: the S24, S24+, and S24 Ultra. The S24 starts at a price of $1,300, the S24+ will cost $1,000, and the S24 will retail at $800.
The South Korean electronics giant showed off the new gadgets at its Kings Cross offices in London earlier this week, prior to the announcement. At a briefing with reporters, Samsung talked up the phone's AI capabilities and showed how it's able to edit pictures and search for items by using AI.
For Samsung's top-tier S24 Ultra, which is the company's biggest of the three devices and comes with punchier specs and features, Samsung is using a version of Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon Series 8 Gen 3 optimized for Galaxy.The company is using its own Exynos chipset for its S24 and S24+ models.
"The Galaxy S24 series devices, together with Google's Pixel range, mark the dawn of the consumerisation of AI in smartphones," Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight, told CNBC. "This is a trend that will be echoed by all smartphone makers, including Apple, as they increasingly add a growing number of AI-powered capabilities to their new devices."
"This launch sees Samsung betting on features powered by artificial intelligence to reignite consumers' interest in smartphones at a time when incremental hardware updates have seen sales slow. Google has been the trailblazer with its Pixel devices and there is little question this is going to be a recurring theme going forward, not just for smartphones but across all consumer electronics."
AI is the name of the game
The Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra is the of the main event for most tech gadget enthusiasts — and, for the most part, it isn't a whole lot different to the Galaxy S23 Ultra looks-wise.
That's because Samsung isn't changing an awful lot with the hardware. It still comes in the same size as its predecessor — the display is 6.8 inches, measured diagonally, though the phone is flatter this time round. The S23 Ultra had more curvature to it.
The big upgrade to the external hardware with this model is that it's cased in titanium, so it's a lot sturdier than the S23 Ultra.
The main difference this time round is what's inside: Samsung is going big on artificial intelligence. A key focus for Samsung, like other smartphone makers, now is on "on-demand" AI — or, the ability to carry out AI workloads directly on a device, rather than over the cloud.
Samsung said its new Galaxy S24 Ultra will come with a bunch of new AI features, a lot of which is being powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chipset for mobile, which is tailored for AI devices.
It signals something that a lot of smartphone makers have been focusing on recently. Consumers aren't getting as excited by new smartphone upgrades as they used to. So phone makers have had to come with ideas to get people's attention again and rev up excitement in the market.
One feature Samsung's loading into the Galaxy S24 range is the ability to circle locations or items a user is directing their camera at, or on a picture they've taken, and then look up results on what those things are.
So, for instance, if you see a landmark or a shoe you want to buy, you can make a circle around that object and then the AI shows you appropriate results on Google.
Another feature Samsung touted is the ability to use AI to edit photos. So users can edit reflections out of pictures they've taken, for instance if you took a picture of yourself in front of a window. Or you can move a person from one side of the room to another by dragging them from left to right.
Samsung also showcased live transcription features with its latest smartphones.
When calling someone who's speaking in French, for instance, a user can pull up a transcription that's being fed through to them in real time. You can also record a conversation between two people and get it transcribed, while the AI assigns a label to each person speaking, similar to transcription products like Otter AI.
Paolo Pescatore, PP Foresight, told CNBC that Samsung "must focus its efforts on retaining its core loyal premium base."
"Arguably [Samsung] has done more than enough with the new features powered by its own AI platform," Pescatoer said. "This potentially could be the start of a new era for smartphone representing a key super cycle for Samsung."
"With this in mind, Samsung will have to entice users with a range of competitor offers to suit everyone; this includes older Samsung owners who will inevitably be looking for a much needed upgrade."
AI watermarking
Another thing Samsung's had to think about is what its AI features mean for things like privacy and copyright infringement.
The past year has seen countless examples of people using AI to create images and other creative media and pass it off as their own work — even when, in some cases, it's derivative from or even looks identical to artists' work.
So when a Galaxy S24 user uses AI to modify a photo, Samsung will keep a log of what was changed with AI and store it in the metadata. It'll also have an icon in the bottom left corner to show that teh image has been edited using AI, kind of like a watermark.
At the Samsung briefing in King's Cross, some analysts and reporters were able to crop this icon out just by using Samsung's in-app cropping feature — though the icon is still kept in the metadata.
"AI-powered image and video manipulation raises some ethical questions, particularly given the recent media attention around deep fake content," Wood told CNBC. "The addition of a watermark and updated metadata for altered content is a constructive step by Samsung and I'm sure others will follow."
"The success of Samsung's AI-based features will largely depend on Samsung's ability to raise consumer awareness and engagement via its marketing for the Galaxy S24 portfolio," he added. "Success will require crisp communication of the benefits and continued expansion of the use cases."

title: Samsung Galaxy S24 lineup goes all in on AI | CNN Business
text: Samsung’s next-generation flagship Galaxy S24 devices aim to take messaging, photos and games to the next level with artificial intelligence. At its annual Samsung Galaxy Unpacked event on Wednesday, the company showed off its Galaxy S24 Ultra, Galaxy S24+ and Galaxy S24 smartphones, in what it says will usher in the next era of how people use their smartphones. The push around AI is part of smartphone makers trying to differentiate themselves in a crowded market and drum up excitement where innovation has largely stalled in recent years. The 6.8-inch Galaxy S24 Ultra ($1,299.99), which will come in a titanium casing for the first time, will be available in various colors including gray, black, violet and yellow. Additional titanium colors including green, blue and orange are available on Samsung.com. The 6.2-inch Galaxy S24 ($799.99) and the 6.7-inch Galaxy S24+ ($999) are available in onyx black, marble gray, cobalt violet and amber yellow. Pre-orders begin Wednesday. By embedding generative AI into the device itself, versus relying on the cloud, Samsung can cut down on lag time and provide better experiences. Its new Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Mobile Platform also makes the most of generative AI and its powerful AI Engine, the company says. “A lot of AI implementation today is somewhat gimmicky, and Samsung, along with other vendors, don’t have a whole lot to gain from adding these features, rather they probably stand to lose more if they were to exclude AI altogether,” said Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at market research firm IDC. The unveiling comes a day after market research firm IDC released data that Apple passed Samsung in smartphone shipments last quarter for the first time. “The last time a company not named Samsung was at the top of the smartphone market was 2010, and for 2023 it is now Apple,” the report said in the release. “A sort of shifting of power at the top of the largest consumer electronics market was driven by an all-time high market share for Apple and a first time at the top.” An AI-packed experience Many of Samsung’s existing features are getting an AI boost. Its suite of live translate products can now translate conversations via a split-screen view while standing next to someone else, providing a transcript in real time. Meanwhile, Samsung’s keyboard will translate messages in real-time in 13 languages. Samsung Notes is also getting an upgrade with pre-made formats to make note jotting more organized. Using generative AI in the car, Android Auto will allow users to request summaries of messages or suggest replies via voice commands. To make online searches more personalized, users can long-hold the home button and circle or tap the screen to learn more about what they see, such as a landmark in the back of someone’s social media page, or ask nuanced questions. Other changes are coming to the camera system. The Galaxy S24 Ultra’s Quad Tele System, with new 5-times optical zoom lens, works with the 50MP sensor to magnify up to 10 times. It also touts upgraded nightography capabilities, and people can use the AI-powered Edit Suggestion tool to make subtle tweaks to photos, such as fixing crooked shots or moving a person or object slightly over to the side. The company said when its devices use generative AI to change an image, a watermark will appear on the image and in metadata. Standing out Although AI on smartphones isn’t entirely new — Google’s latest Pixel 8 lineup launched in October 2023 with many AI features — Samsung’s scale could make more consumers aware of the possibilities. Google’s Pixel line, after all, remains a niche product; its global market share for smartphones remains about 1%, according to data from ABI Research. Ahead of the iPhone 16 launch in September, however, Apple is rumored to be introducing new Siri features, powered by AI in the release of iOS 18. Some on-device generative AI features could be made exclusive to iPhone 16 models, thanks in part to its custom chips. “Apple’s silence on all things AI speaks volumes as many in the industry believe that Apple is potentially lagging,” said IDC’s Ubrani. “That said, none of Samsung’s new AI features will be the primary selling point.”

title: Why AI Can’t Take Away Creative Jobs
text:
This is the published version of Forbes' CMO newsletter, which offers the latest news for chief marketing officers and other messaging-focused leaders. Click here to get it delivered to your inbox every Wednesday.
One of the most pervasive fears about artificial intelligence is that it’s out to take people’s jobs. Generative AI has the ability to write, to create artwork, to make videos with very little human input. And workers are nervous about its possibilities. A CNBC SurveyMonkey Workforce Survey in December found that 60% of employees who regularly use AI fear its impact on their jobs. And last year, Goldman Sachs published a report that estimated 300 million jobs could be displaced by AI automation.
But creativity is a human exercise, and it’s not easily replicated by generative AI. Even though some execs trying to save money may think it’s easy to swap humans for a system that can invent creative ideas, that’s not what people want. A survey done by Wattpad and Wakefield Research found a whopping 92% of people want actual humans involved in writing and producing books. (Meanwhile, the same study found 43% of authors were worried AI could limit monetization and publication opportunities.) Writing books is not the same as conceiving messaging, but it requires a large amount of creativity and human input. And if ordinary readers already seem to know that an AI-generated story would not be something interesting to read, it’s likely they’d also look the other way when presented with an AI-generated campaign.
Deloitte Chief Futurist Mike Bechtel spoke to me a couple of weeks ago about the generative AI trend and how it impacts business. One large theme: AI is a tool to take human innovation to the next level. “This ain’t robots coming for jobs,” he told me. “This is tools used mindfully, changing the world for the better, faster.”
RIGHTS + SPONSORSHIP
Football fans across the United States crowded around their televisions last weekend to watch the NFL Wild Card games. But Saturday night’s game that pitted the Miami Dolphins against the Kansas City Chiefs was the first of its kind. The nationwide broadcast was only available on a streaming service, so most who wanted to watch it needed to be subscribed to NBC’s Peacock. (It was broadcast on local NBC affiliates in the Miami and Kansas City markets, and was also available to users of the NFL+ streaming app.) Comcast, parent company of NBCUniversal, paid $110 million for the exclusive rights to the game.
An average of 23 million viewers tuned in to watch the Chiefs trounce the Dolphins 26-7, making it the most watched live streamed event in U.S. history, according to NBCUniversal. The media giant said the game was responsible for nearly a third of all internet traffic as it was being played, and Peacock was being used on 16.3 million devices at once—which accounts for more than half of its 30 million subscriber base. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell was pleased with the viewership. “To best serve our fans, we need to ensure games are available to them as their viewing habits change and this includes digital distribution as we continue to help shape the future of the sports and entertainment industry,” he said.
Streaming providers have been snapping up rights to broadcast sporting events ranging from NFL games to college basketball. And it’s been reshaping who is able to watch the events, since streaming services can make broadcasts available at any time and in any location. As the NBA works toward negotiating its media rights deal, which expires at the end of the 2024-25 season, it can bring notes on how the NFL has worked out its deals—split between networks and streaming broadcast services (including Amazon Prime, which has no broadcast affiliate)—and copy what’s worked best.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
Another feat for AI: It can bring a legendary comedian back from the dead. Dudesy, a website featuring comedy videos and podcasts, recently released a new hour-long special: George Carlin: I’m Glad I’m Dead. The famed comedian, known for his expletive-laced social commentary, died in 2008. But in the new show, the AI-generated Carlin brings his signature style to 2024, joking about mass shootings and technology. This is the second AI-generated comedy special for Dudesy, the product of Will Sasso and Chad Kultgen. Last year, they released a video “starring” retired NFL quarterback Tom Brady joking about football and dating apps. Brady threatened legal action if Sasso and Kultgen didn’t take the special down. While that specific threat doesn’t exist when the subject of the video is dead, Carlin’s family has been unenthusiastic about the special. “My dad spent a lifetime perfecting his craft from his very human life, brain and imagination. No machine will ever replace his genius,” daughter Kelly Carlin told Forbes contributor Leslie Katz in an email. “These AI-generated products are clever attempts at trying to recreate a mind that will never exist again.”
Fair use of AI was one of the more contentious issues at the heart of the SAG-AFTRA union strikes last year. Actors wanted to ensure their likenesses and voices could not be used without permission, and that they would be fairly compensated for their AI doubles appearing in works. Last week, tensions over AI flared when a deal between the union and AI voice company Replica Studios was announced that would allow digital replicas of members’ voices to be used for video games. The union said this agreement includes provisions including performer consent and negotiations, but many voice actors shared discontent on social media, saying the agreement came without approval of the full union.
FROM THE HEADLINES
It’s 2024 and people have actually started voting in presidential primaries, so it’s safe to say that election season is (actually) on. And while many platforms are taking a stand against AI-generated campaign advertisements, there are several other ways AI can help candidates for offices ranging from local to national in their messaging strategies. AI has already been used for personalized voter targeting, helping candidates to determine what issues matter to individual voters and shaping a candidate’s message to be one to which voters would be most receptive. Algorithms can determine what people are saying about both candidates and the issues on social media, and help pinpoint the best time to send messages to receive maximum impact. AI can help find and engage potential financial donors, as well as analyze and predict polls. The upshot: There’s a lot that AI can do to have a deep impact on the message, without actually generating one.
Larger social platforms say they are ready to moderate election and campaign-related posts. OpenAI says it will ban politicians, campaigns and lobbying groups from using its ChatGPT and Dall-E tools. The generative AI app also says it will introduce authentication tools to prohibit users from impersonating candidates, and help users assess whether to trust images. Meta will label state-run media, require disclosure of AI and other digital tools, and bar campaign ads in the last week of campaigns. Google will limit the types of election-related queries its chatbot Bard and other generative AI products can answer. TikTok says it will work with fact-checking organizations to prevent the spread of misinformation. And X, formerly known as Twitter, will be promoting its crowdsourced fact-checking scheme Community Notes to combat disinformation—though it has been widely criticized as inadequate and error-prone.
DEEP DIVE
A Whole New Shoe Game For Women
As women’s basketball gets more popular, shoe manufacturers are figuring out there’s money to be made—and business to be earned—with signature shoes featuring top WNBA players. While reigning WNBA MVP Breanna Stewart of the New York Liberty learned to play in basketball shoes that either came from the men’s section or were generic, the women MVPs of tomorrow are sporting her signature shoes made by Puma. If they don’t like Stewart’s shoes, they have other options. Liberty’s Sabrina Ionescu and Washington Mystics forward Elena Delle Donne have signature Nike shoes. And Las Vegas Aces forward Candace Parker, a two-time MVP, has a longtime shoe deal with Adidas.
According to Cognitive Market Research, the basketball shoe market was worth $1.38 billion last year. Men’s shoes are currently worth 71% of that market, but analysts expect that balance to shift, reported Forbes’ Justin Birnbaum.
“We’re kind of in a moment here where, for whatever reason, more and more eyes are on women’s basketball,” Max Staiger, Puma’s global head of basketball, told Birnbaum. “That’s directly translating to the interest in products that are associated with everything that comes with that, which is great to see.”
Shoe companies first toed into the women’s basketball arena about 30 years ago, but saw little success. At the time, women’s basketball shoes were seen as inferior products, and customers who bought the newer styles were already customers of the older versions. There was little growth in the sector, and signature shoes and marketing didn’t help sales. It’s a different story today, when more research and customization is making a shoe that better serves women’s unique needs. And in a sign that these shoes are coming full circle, male NBA stars have been seen wearing versions of women’s signature shoes on the court.
FACTS + COMMENTS
Marvel Studios has created movie adaptations of many of its comic book characters, both those who are well-known and some that are relatively undiscovered. Gene Miguel, CEO and cofounder of comic book resale app Shortboxed, said that’s actually boosted the value of comic books.
More than 100,000: Number of users of the Shortboxed app, created about four years ago
$4,750: List price for a 1974 Incredible Hulk comic with the first appearance of Wolverine
‘It’s building a deeper love because it’s on the big screen’: Miguel’s description of movies’ influence

title: Samsung VP James Kitto: How The Galaxy S24 Ultra Heralds A New Age Of Galaxy AI
text:
Samsung calls it "the first dawn of a new age.” With the introduction of Galaxy AI on the Galaxy S24 Ultra, Samsung hopes to leverage the company's enormous scale to bring “the world’s first mobile AI, and put AI into people’s pockets for the first time."
Ahead of the Galaxy S24 launch at Galaxy Unpacked, Samsung UK's VP and Head Of MX, James Kitto, sat down with me to sketch out the vision of Galaxy AI. "Back in 2007, the smartphone market changed forever. In 2024, the AI phone, and what we're bringing to market with the Galaxy S24 is going to rewrite those rules once again."
What's interesting about calling out 2007 is that it represents an inflexion point in the smartphone world, the move away from keypads and unresponsive screens to touchscreens with on-screen buttons and swipeable keyboards. Will 2024's introduction of AI into the consumer experience be as fundamental as the move away from PalmOS and Symbian to iOS and Android?
Manufacturers are certainly pitching this moment as a pivot. It's not just Samsung using AI as a point of differentiation; it is one many manufacturers will likely follow. The days of significant updates to hardware are in the past; the future of hardware will see the spec sheets—at least in raw numbers—look familiar across multiple handsets.
CCS Insight’ Ben Woods highlights why the new Galaxy AI suite is key: “Despite Samsung listing a series of improvements to almost every aspect of its Galaxy S24 family such as the camera, processor, display and more, these days hardware updates do little to move the needle with consumers and reviewers. The big story here is the focus on AI-powered capabilities, which we expect to be the central pillar of Samsung’s marketing for these new devices.”
Samsung is the biggest name so far to commit to this AI Everywhere approach. "We can change the rules," Kitto excitedly tells me. "We can leverage Samsung's scale, with over a billion users. We can present the world's first mobile AI use case to [a massive] market."
The global market for Samsung's Galaxy smartphones is massive. Hanah Securities reports the Galaxy S23 family saw sales of over 25 million units in the first eight months of 2023. The other elephant in the room is Apple. Suppose Tim Cook and his team introduce the presumptively named Apple AI at WWDC 2024 in June and match the sales of the iPhone 14 Pro and 14 Pro (put at 47.5 million sales in the first half of 2023, according to research firm Omdia). In that case, you can expect the iPhone 16 Pro to put up a stiff challenge, depending on Apple’s choices over AI implementation.
For now, Samsung is highlighting several key areas where AI makes a notable difference.
Working around generative and inference tools for text, Android Auto can summarise messages to you, and potential replies while you drive; transcript assist improves on existing speech-to-text tools; and note assist will help both generate notes and also summarise them once they are completed.
Several camera tools have been upgraded thanks to Samsung’s AI-powered ProVisual Engine. It enhances the optical zoom of x5 out to x100; low-light and night-time photography is once again improved through the larger sensors and processing tools, from correcting hand-shakes to interpolating where there is a need for more visual information.
Editing images gains generative editing, filling in any gaps when you edit out objects, adding in a generated scene if you move part of a picture out of frame. The AI tools will also make suggestions on edits to improve your pictures,
That's a long list of just the big-ticket items. What if Kitto had to sell Galaxy AI to an elderly relative and there's time for just one example?
“In that case, it has to be live translate. I travel a lot. I've been sat in the back of taxis trying to explain to a Korean taxi driver where my hotel is, and we've resorted to sign language,” Kitto relates. "So I think the ability to have a communication with someone in their language. That speaks volumes, excuse the pun, to the power of AI."
This raises an important point. AI is a tool for developers; it can't do something it is not programmed to do. Live translate will work in a one-to-one situation, but you're not going to be able to watch the magical musical marathon of Italy's Sanremo and have a Galaxy S24 Ultra offering live translation of the show into English. AI unlocks potential, but it still needs the applications.
While Galaxy AI can handle many tasks locally, some of the more intensive tasks will need to happen in the cloud, with the associated data uploaded for processing. Samsung allows users to opt out of using cloud-based AI services; a toggle in the preferences will limit AI to local services, primarily the inference and prediction engine of Galaxy AI. What you can't do is switch off AI completely; it's part of Samsung's various apps and part of OneUI—Samsung's flavour of Android.
Looking ahead, what is Kitto eager to see? "I'm fascinated by the consumer demand; the channel partners’ expectations for this launch are as big as I’ve ever seen."
AI makes a difference, but thanks to science fiction, Artifical Intelligence is a loaded term. Using tools to infer what could come next in a sentence or could be hiding behind a bush in a picture is a far cry from HAL 9000 locking you out of your home. Yet AI is the term we have, so we will have AI everywhere, even if the practical uses are one step removed from the expectations.
When someone wants a phone with AI, Samsung wants to be first in line with the Galaxy S24, Galaxy S24+, and Galaxy S24 Ultra.

title: Out Of The Doghouse: CMOs Make Striking Comeback In Latest CEO Survey
text:
In a dramatic reversal from recent years, CEOs are gaining new confidence in their chief marketing officers (CMOs), according to the latest CEO survey from Boathouse.
CMOs Score by Delivering on CEO Priorities
The study, now in its third year, polled 150 CEOs of major U.S. companies on their views towards marketing and CMOs. In the past, the results painted a gloomy picture - in 2021, only 20% of CEOs rated their company's marketing capability as "best in class." Just 21% gave their CMO an A grade.
But the tide has clearly turned. This year, fully half of CEOs now rate their marketing department as "best in class." The number of CMOs earning an A grade has also jumped substantially, to 40%.
Behind this reversal: CEOs say CMOs are delivering on core business priorities. Nearly 9 in 10 CEOs believe their CMO understands and takes action on their vision. CMO scores are way up in driving growth, innovation, analytics, and other areas CEOs value most.
Trust and Loyalty Growing Between CMOs and CEOs
Trust is growing too. 69% of CEOs place CMOs in their "top tier" of trusted advisors, on par with CFOs and COOs. And, they perceive CMOs as loyal to the company, if not always the CEO personally.
This is good news for CMOs. Last year, the tenure of CMOs at the top 100 advertisers fell to its lowest value in a decade, a mere 39 months. By comparison, the average tenure of a CEO is 7.2 years.
For the first time, a majority of CEOs in the study said they were aware of the short CMO tenure issue. Even more dramatically, 51% of CEOs view short CMO tenure as an indicator of success. Just one year earlier, 81% thought short tenure was a sign of failure.
CMOs Making Strides on Strategy and Financials
Two areas where CMOs have traditionally struggled are strategic thinking and financial literacy. But, the latest survey shows improvement.
While CEOs still give lower grades to CMOs in "ability to drive strategy" versus other competencies, the numbers have notably increased. The percentage of CMOs earning an A grade for strategy has doubled since last year, from 16% to 31%.
On finances, 69% of CEOs now say their CMO understands the P&L and balance sheet, up substantially from 53% two years ago. Though fewer than half participate directly in setting financial goals, involvement is trending up.
So while strategy and finance remain relative weak spots, CEOs perceive that CMOs are making real progress. This is an encouraging sign, as CEOs need marketing leaders who can connect the dots between strategic vision, financial outcomes, and market execution.
CMOs Lean Into AI, CEOs Approve
Artificial intelligence adoption is a top priority for CEOs, and their CMOs seem to be getting the message.
The study found marketing has the broadest AI integration across the organization. 58% of CEOs say their CMO has made AI presentations, requests, or implemented new AI processes in the past year.
When asked to grade their CMO's ability with AI and machine learning, over half of CEOs gave an A or B. They view AI as a way for marketing to drive innovation and efficiency.
Early AI applications in marketing focus on content generation, personalization, analytics, customer experience, and research. While still nascent, CMOs are clearly making AI a priority. And CEOs are on board - 90% believe their CMO is pursuing AI to benefit the business, not just their career.
Not Time for a CMO Victory Lap
Despite the positive news for CMOs, challenges clearly remain in maximizing marketing's business impact. But the survey signals a meaningful reversal in C-suite perceptions. As marketing takes on existential threats like AI, privacy, and fragmentation, CMOs are, at least for the moment, back in the CEO's good graces.

title: Samsung vies to make AI more mainstream by baking in more of the technology in its new Galaxy phones
text:
Samsung vies to make AI more mainstream by baking in more of the technology in its new Galaxy phones
Smartphones could get much smarter this year as the next wave of artificial intelligence seeps into the devices that accompany people almost everywhere they go
SAN JOSE, Calif. -- Smartphones could get much smarter this year as the next wave of artificial intelligence seeps into the devices that accompany people almost everywhere they go.
Samsung, the biggest rival to Apple and its iPhone, provided a glimpse of how smartphones are evolving during a Wednesday unveiling of the next generation of its flagship Galaxy models.
The sales pitch for the Galaxy S24 lineup revolves around an array of new features powered by AI.
“We will reshape the technology landscape, we will open a new chapter without barriers to unleash your potential," TM Roh, the president of Samsung's mobile experience division, vowed to a crowd gathered in a San Jose, California, arena usually used for hockey games and concerts.
Besides featuring some of Samsung's own work in AI, the Galaxy S24 lineup will be packed with some of the latest advances coming out of Google.
The technological improvements will also usher in a higher price for Samsung's top-of-the-line phone, the Galaxy S24 Ultra, which will be priced at $1,300 — a $100, or 8% increase, from last year's comparable model. The increase mirrors what Apple did with its fanciest model, the iPhone 15 Pro Max, released in September.
Samsung is holding steady on the prices for the Galaxy S24 Plus, which will sell for $1,000, and the basic Galaxy S24, which will start at $800.
All the new Galaxy phones, due in stores Jan. 31, will be packed with far more AI than before, including a feature that will provide live translation during phone calls in 13 languages and 17 dialects. The Galaxy S24 lineup will also introduce Google's “Circle To Search” that involves using a digital stylus or a finger to circle snippets of text, parts of photos or videos to get instant search results about whatever has been highlighted.
The new Galaxy phones will also enable quick and easy ways to manipulate the appearance and placement of specific parts of pictures taken on the devices' camera. It's a feature that could help people refine their photos, while also making it easier to create misleading images.
Google started a push last fall to infuse its latest Pixel phones with more AI, including the ability to alter the appearance of photos — an effort that the company accelerated at the end of last year with the initial rollout of project Gemini, its next technological leap. Google is also pushing out the Circle To Search tool to its latest phones, the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro, with plans to expand it to other devices running on its Android software later this year.
Besides introducing Circle To Search, Google also is drawing upon AI to enable users of its mobile app for iPhones as well as Android to point a camera at an object for a summary about what is being captured by the lens. Although Google believes Circle To Search and the Lens option will make its results even more useful, executives have also acknowledged they both may be prone to inaccuracies.
Like virtually all phone manufacturers other than Apple, Samsung relies on Google's Android operating system, so the two companies' interests have been aligned even though they compete against each other in the sale of mobile devices.
Apple is expected to put more AI into its next generation of iPhones in September, but now Samsung has a head start toward gaining the upper hand in making the technology more ubiquitous, Forrester Research analyst Thomas Husson said. It's a competitive edge that Samsung could use, having ceded its longstanding mantle as the world's largest seller of smartphones to Apple last year, according to the market research firm International Data Corp.
“Samsung’s marketing challenge is precisely to make the technology transparent to impress consumers with magic and invisible experiences,” Husson said.
The increasing use of AI in smartphones comes after the Microsoft-backed startup, OpenAI, thrust the technology into the mainstream last year with its ChatGPT bot capable of quickly creating stories, memos, videos and drawings upon request.
As AI becomes a more integral piece of smartphones, the technology will likely have broad implications on productivity, creativity and privacy, predicted Todd Lohr, U.S. technology consulting leader for KPMG.
“Intelligence is actually coming to your smartphone, which really haven't been that smart,” Lohr said. “You may eventually see use cases where you could have your smartphone listen to you all day and have it provide a summary of your day at the end of it. That could create a challenge in the social construct because if everyone's device is listening to everyone, whose data is it?”
AI isn't quite that advanced yet, but Samsung already is trying to address privacy worries likely to be raised by the amount of new technology rolling out in the Galaxy S24 lineup. Samsung executives are emphasizing that the AI features can be kept on the device, although some applications may need to connect to data centers in the virtual cloud.
The South Korean company also is promising users that their on-device activity will be protected by its “Samsung Knox” security.
Michael Kokotajlo, KPMG's digital transformation partner of telecommunications, thinks Samsung and other smartphone makers are on the way to giving people an “AI assistant in their pockets” — a concept that he expects to be more readily adopted by younger generations that have grown up during the mobile-computing era.
“Millennials and Gen Z are definitely going to be looking for these AI capabilities because they don’t have as much concern about privacy and security, but some of the older generations may have more concerns about that or how do you even leverage all of it,” Kokotajlo said.

title: Ramaswamy proposes debate with Harris on AI as speculation swirls over Trump's running mate
text:
Ramaswamy proposes debate with Harris on AI as speculation swirls over Trump's running mate
Vivek Ramaswamy heard chants of 'VP' at a New Hampshire Trump rally
Vivek Ramaswamy proposed that Vice President Harris debate him on the topic of artificial intelligence, as speculation over former President Trump's choice of running mate swirls.
"Kamala is in charge of AI policy right now. In a debate, I’d challenger [sic] her to see if she can spell ‘AI.’ I’d bet on the same blank stare I got from Nikki when I asked her to name 3 provinces in eastern Ukraine," Ramaswamy wrote Tuesday night, referencing a moment from a GOP debate in December.
Ramaswamy's post challenging Harris came in response to Human Events senior editor Jack Posobiec writing, "Imagine what Vivek would do to Kamala in a debate."
In November, Harris notably gave a speech on the future of artifical intelligence in London, vowing that, the "United States will continue to work with the G7; the United Nations; and a diverse range of governments, from the Global North to the Global South, to promote AI safety and equity around the world."
VIVEK RAMASWAMY URGES DESANTIS AND HALEY TO DROP OUT OF RACE
Just days earlier, speaking from the East Room of the White House, Harris also warned, "AI can lead to discrimination, bias and other abuses," vowing to work with civil rights leaders.
Harris added that the "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights," an administration document that recommends "proactive equity assessments as part of the system design," would establish "a minimum baseline of responsible AI practices" for private companies operating within the field.
KAMALA HARRIS: ADMIN HAS DUTY TO STOP AI 'ALGORITHMIC DISCRIMINATION,' ENSURE BENEFITS 'SHARED EQUITABLY'
Her comments came after the American Accountability Foundation (AAF), a conservative watchdog group, had recently warned the Biden administration was actively seeking to use AI to promote woke, progressive ideology with left-wing activists leading the effort.
In another post on X on Wednesday, Ramaswamy reiterated his call for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Haley to join him in suspending their 2024 presidential campaigns following Trump’s commanding victory at the Iowa caucuses.
"It’s time to move forward," Ramaswamy wrote. "Running the race through Iowa was fair game. But the people have spoken loud & clear. The game is over. We have a country to save."
"Last night, I asked all my supporters across New Hampshire who’ve *run through walls* for me to do one LAST thing this week: volunteer all-out for the next 6 days to make sure Trump defeats Nikki by *as wide of a margin* as possible. End this primary & do what’s right for America," he wrote in another post.
Ramaswamy bowed out of the race after coming in fourth at the caucuses Monday night, and immediately endorsed Trump.

Trump has yet to announce his choice of 2024 running mate but told Fox News during a town hall last week his mind was already made up.
