Anthropic fires back at music publishers' AI copyright lawsuit
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic asks Tennessee federal court to reject music publishers' bid to stop it from using song lyrics in its chatbot Claude; Anthropic argues that publishers failed to prove irreparable harm and brought lawsuit in wrong court. Many copyright owners including authors, visual artists and the New York Times have sued tech companies such as Meta Platforms and Microsoft-backed OpenAI over the use of their work to train generative-AI systems.
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic has asked a Tennessee federal court to reject an early bid by three music publishers to stop it from using and reproducing their song lyrics through its chatbot Claude.
Anthropic told the court on Tuesday that Universal Music , ABKCO and Concord Music Group could not prove they were being irreparably harmed. It also argued that the publishers had brought their lawsuit against the company in the wrong court.
The publishers' attorney Matt Oppenheim said on Wednesday that they were confident in their request and "believe that Anthropic's infringement should be stopped."
Representatives for Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the filing.
Many copyright owners including authors, visual artists and the New York Times have sued tech companies such as Meta Platforms and Microsoft-backed OpenAI over the use of their work to train generative-AI systems.
The music publishers' lawsuit, filed last October, appears to be the first over song lyrics and the first against Anthropic, which has drawn financial backing from Google , Amazon and former cryptocurrency mogul Sam Bankman-Fried.
The complaint accused Anthropic of infringing the publishers' copyrights in lyrics from at least 500 songs by musicians including Beyonce, the Rolling Stones and The Beach Boys. The publishers claim Anthropic misused the lyrics as part of the "massive amounts of text" that it scrapes from the internet to train Claude to respond to human prompts.
The publishers asked the court in November for a preliminary injunction to block the use of their copyrighted material to train Claude and force the company to implement "guardrails" against reproducing their lyrics.
Anthropic responded on Wednesday that it already has guardrails to prevent Claude from generating copyrighted material.
"If those measures failed in some instances in the past, that would have been a 'bug,' not a 'feature,' of the product," Anthropic said.
The company also argued that there was "no evidence" that any other Claude users "entered prompts that resulted in Plaintiffs' lyrics being shown to them."
"Normal people would not use one of the world's most powerful and cutting-edge generative AI tools to show them what they could more reliably and quickly access using ubiquitous web browsers," Anthropic said.
The company also said it was "confident" that its AI training makes fair use of copyrighted material and would show how the publishers' case "misconceives the technology and the law alike."
The case is Concord Music Group Inc v. Anthropic PBC, U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, No. 3:23-cv-01092.

title: Huawei sets up new smart car company as autos business takes off | CNN Business
text: Huawei has set up a separate smart car unit, in another stride forward in the Chinese tech giant’s plans to make a splash in the automotive world. The company incorporated Shenzhen Yinwang Intelligent Technology Co Ltd on Tuesday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Huawei is based. The new firm is wholly owned by Huawei and will focus on the “manufacturing and sales of intelligent car systems and equipment,” according to Tianyancha and Qichacha, two corporate data providers in China. The business has registered initial capital of 1 billion yuan (about $140.5 million) and shares the same address as Huawei’s headquarters, according to the data providers. The news marks another milestone for Huawei, which has accelerated its automotive ambitions in the past three years. The Chinese group originally made its name as a tech and telecoms giant, selling smartphones, consumer devices and network equipment. But it has been hobbled in recent years by US export restrictions, which sent the company into a tailspin. More recently, it has made no secret of its ambition to make a comeback. In 2021, it jumped into the electric vehicle (EV) race, launching its first battery-powered vehicle. Last year, it also rolled out two new vehicles to great fanfare in China, including its first electric sedan, the Luxeed S7, designed to take on Elon Musk’s Tesla (TSLA). That was followed by the December debut of the Aito M9, an electric SUV targeting high-end buyers. The unveiling coincided with a launch by Chinese rival Xiaomi of its own first electric car, showing how competition between the two companies has spilled over to another sector. The new vehicles have added to China’s crowded auto market, the world’s largest, which has seen a price war in recent months due to fierce competition and high inventories. Huawei’s new business, however, appears to already have won a big backer. In November, a subsidiary of Changan, a Chinese state-owned automaker, disclosed that it had partnered with Huawei to form a new company created to provide smart car systems. According to a filing made to the Shenzhen stock exchange by Chongqing Changan Automobile Co, Huawei would set up the firm, which would focus on digital platforms inside the car and other automotive systems and components. Changan plans to take a stake of up to 40% in the business, which it hopes to help further its goals of becoming a low-carbon, tech-driven transportation company, it said in the filing. Huawei and Changan did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday. It’s unclear whether Shenzhen Yinwang is part of the November agreement. AI cars Smart cars, which refer to vehicles that use advanced software systems or electronics, are becoming more common as tech firms increasingly team up with automakers. Huawei, for instance, offers a software system for vehicles called HarmonyOS for Automotive, which is designed to sync with its mobile operating system of the same name and “create a seamless experience across nearby devices,” according to the company. This week, BYD, the Chinese carmaker backed by Warren Buffett, also made headlines by introducing Xuanji, an AI-powered system for cars. The software is designed to make driving safer and more comfortable by responding to “changes in the internal and external environment of the car,” the company said in a Tuesday statement. The news comes as China is racing forward on its development of advanced technology, particularly artificial intelligence. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology unveiled draft guidelines that sought to standardize the country’s fast-moving AI industry. Under the planned rules, China aims to form at least 50 nationwide and industry-wide standards for AI by 2026, and participate in forming at least 20 international standards for AI by that year. The government also wants to have at least 1,000 companies adopt and apply these standards by 2026, the ministry said. China has been one of the first countries in the world to regulate the space, having published rules for generative AI last July. The rules, designed to oversee the software behind popular services like ChatGPT, took effect in August. Since then, China has raced to keep pace with the United States on the burgeoning technology. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in Switzerland on Tuesday, a US lawmaker said that the country measured its lead over competitors in AI in “months,” highlighting the breakneck speed of development in the sector.

title: AI is the buzz, the big opportunity and the risk to watch among the Davos glitterati
text:
AI is the buzz, the big opportunity and the risk to watch among the Davos glitterati
Artificial intelligence is easily the biggest buzzword for world leaders and corporate bosses diving into big ideas at the World Economic Forum’s glitzy annual meeting in Davos
DAVOS, Switzerland -- Artificial intelligence is easily the biggest buzzword for world leaders and corporate bosses diving into big ideas at the World Economic Forum’s glitzy annual meeting in Davos. Breathtaking advances in generative AI stunned the world last year, and the elite crowd is angling to take advantage of its promise and minimize its risks.
In a sign of ChatGPT maker OpenAI’s skyrocketing profile, CEO Sam Altman is making his Davos debut to rock star crowds, with his benefactor, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, hot on his heels.
Illustrating AI’s geopolitical importance like few other technologies before it, the word was on the lips of world leaders from China to France. It was visible across the Swiss Alpine town and percolated through afterparties.
Here's a look at the buzz:
The leadership drama at the AI world's much-ballyhooed chatbot maker followed Altman and Nadella to the swanky Swiss snows.
Altman, who was suddenly fired last year by OpenAI’s board and then swiftly reinstated, said at a Bloomberg event that he was focused on getting a “great full board in place” and would consider changes down the road to the company’s unusual structure, which is governed by a nonprofit.
He deflected further questions, interrupting a question directed at an OpenAI executive accompanying him by saying, “Is really what you want to spend our time on the soap opera rather than what AGI is going to do?”
AGI is artificial general intelligence, a term for the better-than-human AI technology OpenAI is seeking to build. With that on the horizon, Altman talked technology and humanity on a panel Thursday.
Nadella, meanwhile, said, “I’m comfortable, I have no issues with any structure” of the operating model at OpenAI, the startup Microsoft has poured billions into. At another Bloomberg event, he noted that “what I would like is good governance and real stability.”
Forum founder Klaus Schwab quizzed the Microsoft CEO on whether world leaders were up to the task of creating AI regulations but steered well clear of questions about OpenAI's governance.
From China to Europe, top officials staked their positions on AI as the world grapples with regulating the rapidly developing technology that has big implications for workplaces, elections and privacy.
The European Union has devised the world's first comprehensive AI rules ahead of a busy election year, with AI-powered misinformation and disinformation the biggest risk to the global economy as it threatens to erode democracy and polarize society, according to a World Economic Forum report released last week.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang called AI “a double-edged sword.”
“Human beings must control the machines instead of having the machines control us,” he said in a speech Tuesday. “AI must be guided in a direction that is conducive to the progress of humanity, so there should be a redline in AI development — a red line that must not be crossed,” without elaborating.
China, one of the world’s centers of AI development, wants to “step up communication and cooperation with all parties” on improving global AI governance, Li said.
China has released interim regulations for managing generative AI, but the EU broke ground with its AI Act, which won a hard-fought political deal last month and awaits final sign-off.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said AI is "a very significant opportunity, if used in a responsible way.”
She said “the global race is already on” to develop and adopt AI, and touted the 27-nation EU's efforts, including the AI Act and a program pairing supercomputers with small and midsized businesses to train large AI models.
French President Emmanuel Macron said he's a “strong believer” in AI and that his country is “an attractive and competitive country” for the industry. He played up France's role in helping coordinate regulation on deepfake images and videos created with AI as well as plans to host a follow-up summit on AI safety after an inaugural gathering in Britain in October.
The letters “AI” were omnipresent along the Davos Promenade, where consulting firms and tech giants are among the groups that swoop onto the main drag each year, renting out shops and revamping them into showcase pavilions.
Inside the main conference center, a giant digital wall emanated rolling images of AI art and computer-generated conceptions of wildlife and nature like exotic birds or tropical streams.
Davos-goers who wanted to delve more deeply into the technical ins and outs of artificial intelligence could drop in to sessions at the AI House.
Generative AI systems like ChatGPT and Google's Bard captivated the world by rapidly spewing out new poems, images and computer code and are expected to have a sweeping impact on life and work.
The technology could help give a boost to the stagnating global economy, said Nadella, whose company is rolling out the technology in its products.
The Microsoft chief said he's “very optimistic about AI being that general purpose technology that drives economic growth."
Business leaders predicted AI will help automate mundane work tasks or make it easier for people to do advanced jobs, but they also warned that it would threaten workers who can’t keep up.
A survey of 4,700 CEOs in more than 100 countries by PwC, released at the start of the Davos meetings, said 14% think they'll have to lay off staff because of the rise of generative AI.
“There isn’t an area, there isn’t an industry that’s not going to be impacted” by AI, said Julie Sweet, CEO of consulting firm Accenture.
For those who can move with the change, AI promises to transform tasks like computer coding, customer relations and streamline business functions like invoicing, IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said.
“If you embrace AI, you’re going to make yourself a lot more productive,” he said. “If you do not ... you’re going to find that you do not have a job.”
During a session featuring Meta chief AI scientist Yann LeCun, talk about risks and regulation led to the moderator's hypothetical example of “infinitely conversant sexbots” that could be built by anyone using open source technology.
Taking the high road, LeCun replied that AI can’t be dominated by a handful of Silicon Valley tech giants AI if it’s going to serve people around the world with different languages, cultures and values.
“You do not want this to be under the control of a small number of private companies,” he said.

title: Council Post: The True Value Of AI Lies In The Wisdom Of Its Application
text:
Chairman & Chief Executive Officer of Emergn.
Worldwide, across both public and private spheres of influence, AI is turbocharging products and services. In fact, data from my company reveals that in four years, 94% of new digital products and services are projected to be created using AI.
This trend underscores AI’s expanding reach into global product and service development, surpassing many current expectations. However, as AI becomes more integral to business operations, leaders face the challenge of understanding and managing potential risks. The question arises: Have leaders sufficiently grasped the extent of these risks to prepare effectively? Currently, there is no established regulatory framework or widely accepted best practices.
Unanswered questions abound as to the implications of AI use on data privacy, accuracy and scalability, while return on investment is far from certain in all cases. To address these challenges and make sure AI tools are used ethically, I believe that organizations need to create strong frameworks to supervise these tools—with a specific focus on the data used for its training.
Overall, successful AI implementation will require a combination of expertise sharing, continuous learning and a shift in leadership mindset.
AI's Productivity Surge
Stanford University's AI Index shows a consistent annual growth rate in global corporate investment since 2011. Major tech players like Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, along with emerging startups, continue to fuel innovation in this field. In the public sphere, AI is enhancing productivity in manufacturing, optimizing supply chains and enabling intelligent cargo routing with autonomous vehicles. I predict widespread disruption in critical areas like infrastructure, healthcare, education and public services.
Recent political party conferences in the U.K. highlight the potential impact—from Network North to National Grid overhauls. The world’s first AI Security Summit hosted by the U.K. last month further confirms AI’s increasingly indispensable role across global businesses.
Three Barriers To Success
However, I believe that the potential for continued value creation hinges on three factors identified in my company's research: data privacy, accurate results and scalability.
Safeguards for collating sensitive information involve developing comprehensive protocols and ethical frameworks to ensure transparency and accountability throughout the process. We also need to make sure that AI delivers accurate results. A focus on precision can help minimize errors, reduce costs and ensure compliance with regulations.
Lastly, scalability poses challenges in handling the increased scale of data and processing involved with AI tools. Unless the AI-powered product can increase/decrease complexity, size or speed at scale to handle customer and business requirements appropriately, ultimately, it's of limited use.
While AI holds transformative potential, it necessitates responsibility and ethical grounding. It is important for leaders to establish robust procedures to integrate AI into operational practices, leverage experienced development teams and cultivate their leadership skills for optimizing returns on AI investments.
Return On Investment: Is AI Worth The Risk?
Identifying, developing and deploying the right AI infrastructures in a safe, ethical and sustainable way will require investment—both in time and finances.
This can seem off-putting to business leaders who may be either impatient to unlock AI or fear the return on investment (ROI) is far from certain. This was shown in KMPG’s recent generative AI survey, which found that 45% of business executives remained concerned about the potential of the technology to impact their organization negatively and, in turn, stakeholder trust.
In 2020, research firm ESI ThoughtLab published a study "exploring how companies are approaching their AI implementations, what value they are seeking, and what they are achieving." They discovered that individuals achieving a significant return on investment for their AI projects (exceeding 5%) had adopted essential practices related to data management. Therefore, I think the primary concern should be focusing on data management and looking to enhance that 5% figure for improved performance.
A Blueprint For Successful AI Implementation
Achieving true transformation with AI involves a blend of expertise sharing and continuous learning to challenge obsolete mindsets and adapt to new technologies. Success in AI implementation is not solely about being tech-savvy; it's equally about training colleagues in effective methodologies. Overlooking this aspect can result in long-term setbacks.
Working with many businesses who are on this journey, my recommendations for effective AI applications are:
1. Seek effectiveness before efficiencies.
While efficiency is about process optimization and resource reduction, effectiveness targets strategic goal achievement and delivering significant outcomes. Companies should align AI implementations with their broader business goals, focusing on addressing specific challenges or creating innovative solutions.
2. Focus on outcomes.
AI implementation should aim to achieve specific, tangible goals, whether enhancing customer experiences, optimizing decision-making or innovating products and services. This strategy not only improves long-term success but also fosters a culture of continuous improvement, adaptability and innovation.
3. Identify and exploit bottlenecks.
Bottlenecks represent opportunities for innovation and optimization. Companies should use these constraints as focal points for improvement and experimentation.
4. Increase the rate of feedback.
In a recent survey of product and IT leaders that my company conducted, 80% of respondents were concerned that "rule by committee" is blocking innovation with too many decision-makers in the process, reducing feedback and collaboration. Implementing effective feedback strategies can foster a culture of continuous improvement and responsiveness. Strategies include A/B testing for real-world comparison of AI models and defining and tracking relevant KPIs to measure AI implementation success and pinpoint areas for enhancement.
The true value of AI is not found in its technical prowess but rather in the comprehensive way in which it is applied across the entire enterprise. Investing in responsible AI infrastructures, prioritizing data management and adopting essential practices are crucial for optimal returns and true transformation.

title: Council Post: AI: Who's Governing It, And Who Should Be?
text:
Chief Strategy Officer at Zoho Corporation overseeing strategy, channels, account management and various marketing and operational efforts.
At the 2023 World Economic Forum, a group of chief risk officers produced the inaugural Chief Risk Officers Outlook, a survey of factors that could increase "the likely level of global volatility" around the globe. AI was, unsurprisingly, chief among them.
Despite a lack of governance, the use of generative AI has exponentially escalated beyond what even this collection of CROs could imagine. Take ChatGPT, for example: According to Reuters, the number of users grew from 100 million in January 2023 to 180.5 million by August 2023. The appetite for AI in the workplace is growing, and soon, users won't have much of a choice about whether it will be part of their work, as it will be arriving standard with all software packages.
At our software company, we've prioritized the surgical integration of a generative AI assistant into our software to elevate the work customers are already doing. AI-driven tasks like synthesizing data or streamlining a task pipeline lay the groundwork for an effective employee. Our measured approach requires understanding where governance is headed and how its shortcomings can lead to issues with privacy and security.
Here's more on regulating something that defies regulations.
The Problem With Privacy
Once AI is fully calibrated to a company's infrastructure, it can offer robust protection from cyberattacks and data breaches. Beforehand, AI requires access to a significant amount of sensitive information, particularly throughout the training process. For AI to be effective, it has to swim in a pool that people regularly fill with information, and that can be invasive.
Companies and consumers are voicing their fears: The future is inevitable, and a majority of tech folks aren't ready. Our company's Generative AI Adoption in the Workplace study, which surveyed 4,540 global workers across six countries in August 2023, found that 84% of U.S. respondents believe generative AI will become an ingrained, openly accepted part of their job within the next year. At the same time, 81% of U.S. respondents voiced concerns about how AI exposes their data.
Vendors seeking to lead should put privacy forward as a competitive differentiator, diverting resources into building the most secure software possible. Simultaneously, these companies can revisit their privacy policies and ensure they're customer-facing. If a company's AI requires first-party data to improve its processes, it should let potential customers know. We've found that users are savvy to the language of privacy. Have faith in their intelligence; there exists an exponential relationship between transparency and trust.
The Problem With Security
AI can monitor itself for odd behavior indicative of a cyberattack and take swift action when required. The problem is that sometimes, action can do more harm than good. Due to hiccups like corrupted data, savvy phishing attempts and lack of unification, a company's AI can quickly become a liability.
Companies must remember that AI is still a piece of software that can become outdated or abused. Some pieces of AI can mitigate this danger by pushing security updates across the ecosystem, not simply a few of the apps, but that's not enough. Motivated hackers will stay ahead of the update curve and find a way to disrupt the software.
Companies have to treat AI less like Skynet and more like a team member who, while reliable, still has flaws—many of which are buried deep within the code. This necessitates a human fail-safe baked into the process that can monitor alerts and suss out which are false positives, which are legitimate security threats, and which demonstrate odd behavior that may be indicative of future threats in the making.
Regulations: It's Already Too Late
In theory, governance and regulations surrounding AI would instill trust among consumers. Unfortunately, some consumers are entirely unaware of their existence. And even so, outside of the European Union and a handful of states in the U.S., governance is mostly nonexistent, and what little does exist is in its nascent stages: California's—the first—was established only a few years ago, in 2020. Most other states have only passed the laws; they haven't yet taken effect.
Some progress is being made. India recently passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which will go into effect at a yet-to-be-determined point in the future. Four more U.S. states have recently introduced new legislation for consideration. Still, AI is evolving at such a rapid rate that it's impossible for governments and regulators to keep up. According to the CRO Outlook report, 43% of CRO respondents feel that the development of AI technology should slow while regulations catch up, and 90% feel regulations need to accelerate regardless.
It might not make much of a difference. While OpenAI's ChatGPT is trained on publicly available data, private models built from proprietary data, like BloombergGPT, are difficult to regulate, and more private LLMs arrive each month. Governance, then, falls to the vendors—a dicey proposition, at best.
Companies can stifle distrust by providing consumer education opportunities. When a tech company messes up, customers are the ones left holding the bag, so it behooves them to be fully informed before embracing a particular vendor and its proprietary LLM. The dangers of bad actors might not make it worth chasing that elusive ROI. Customer behavior should be guiding governance, not the other way around.
Biden's Executive Order: What It Means Moving Forward
As one of my colleagues recently said to Solutions Review, the Biden administration's recent executive order on AI demonstrates that when vendors don't police themselves, which is to be expected, regulations will attempt to do the policing. Unfortunately, governments will always play catchup to technology evolving faster than it can be reined in, and this executive order fails to enable the full level of transparency needed to predict where the technology is headed.
Instead, tech companies need to see this announcement as a call to institute their own AI best practices and communicate them to consumers who, through their purchase decisions, will serve as the true regulators of AI moving forward. It's also important that those consumers understand how government agencies will use AI—an area not covered by the executive order. We are in the initial stages of an AI revolution, and my hope is that governance, or lack thereof, doesn't slow the innovation process.

title: Council Post: The Future Of AI Is In Augmentation, Not Annihilation
text:
Cofounder and CEO of Adverity.
Few figures illustrate—or vocalize—the AI paradox better than Elon Musk. At the U.K. 2023 AI Safety Summit, Musk warned that advanced technology could replace "all human jobs" and compared it to a "'magic genie' capable of granting unlimited wishes," with these comments coming after the launch of X.ai, his own "hyper-intelligent AI business."
Such workforce concerns raised so far aren’t entirely far-fetched. Following numerous predictions about AI development, research shows that "half of today’s work activities could be automated between 2030 and 2060." Yet, as highlighted at the summit, these extremes remain hypothetical and there's still plenty of time to avoid them by making AI what U.K. Prime Minster Rishi Sunak calls a helpful “co-pilot” to humanity.
Even if machines do take on a large chunk of human workloads, such increased business integration doesn’t have to hurt (or replace) employees. The key factor that companies must prioritize is balance.
Using innovations responsibly to streamline select everyday tasks will enable AI-assisted augmentation, not team annihilation, by helping workers win back precious time and achieve better productivity. Or, to quote the optimistic vision of HubSpot cofounder and CTO, Dharmesh Shah: “AI will take your job and give you one that’s much better. One that involves less cranking and more creativity, less grind, and more growth, one where you have superpowers.”
The Growing Gains Of Intelligent Tech
Continuing hype about generative AI offerings isn’t surprising, mostly because of their newly honed abilities to process more data and multitask faster. This is especially true in cases in which tools hit what Deloitte researchers call the usage “sweet spot,” where they can handle tasks that would require high human effort and produce easily checked outputs. But it’s also important to recognize the long-running efficiency benefits of other smart solutions, particularly when it comes to data organization.
With businesses increasingly looking to guide decisions at every level using comprehensive insight, automated orchestration has played a vital role in supporting workers, enabling them to handle expanding data sources and the challenges they bring. Tools that can quickly collect, merge and unify multiple data strains have already saved hours of manual collation, sorting and assessment, in addition to reducing the risk of human error.
More recently, leaps forward in data mapping and quality monitoring have also made it easier to get data in actionable shape with the auto-matching of cross-platform metrics and dimensions. This provides harmonized values that employees can use to interrogate holistic datasets, and auto-flagging of similar data under different labels enables them to rapidly find and fix discrepancies. This may explain why Microsoft research (paywall) has found that employees are pro-tech assistance, as long as it presents clear positives, with tools capable of covering repetitive tasks and steering better (data-driven) choices among the top picks they want businesses to adopt.
Embracing The Power Of Collaboration
In the near term, functionalities expected to best answer workforce prayers might not necessarily sound revolutionary. Although data sophistication has progressed significantly over the past few years, the reality is that many firms aren’t ready for leading-edge tech solutions, as evidenced by the fact that half are still driving decisions using a mix of data and gut feeling.
The area that stands to gain the most from the increased application of wider intelligent tools and generative AI (GenAI) is core data coordination, specifically on two main fronts:
1. Making Data Malleable
AI has huge potential to improve data mobility and pliability—in other words, giving users more control. At the basic level, tools that deploy traditional instruction-led algorithms can play a major part in helping users make data pipelines work for them by applying custom rules and logic. Practical examples of this may include using AI processing engines as "data to order" services, such as setting data retrieval frequencies, timeframes and configurations.
Stepping things up a notch, using tech with an array of pre-loaded transformation options allows individuals to fine-tune how incoming data is structured to suit their unique usage needs, without requiring coding expertise. And going even further, the latest GenAI-powered analytics can also produce custom code in line with bespoke specifications. Along with saving valuable time for data analysts and specialists, such malleability will mean every user can get their data formatting wish and start putting the right insights into action.
2. Serving Up Vital Insights
Once firms have reached intermediate data and AI proficiency, the next big (worker-friendly) focus is likely to be augmented analytics. Bringing together a host of AI techniques—such as statistical modeling, machine learning and data mining—this concept is about deep diving. Assessing vast stores of fresh and historic data using self-learning AI algorithms, augmented systems model multiple factors—from long-term customer behavior and business revenue to real-time competitor activity—and identify key trends, patterns and anomalies.
From the employee standpoint, outputted insights not only quickly and accurately pinpoint how their efforts are performing but also identify which opportunities and challenges need addressing. Combined with GenAI features that give them the capacity to ask for custom summaries and visualizations of specific datasets, the result is an accessible view of exactly what's happening and what they should do next, minus the usual intensive data wrangling.
The core moral of the story here is simple: Just because technology can achieve tasks once seen as the remit of humans doesn’t mean it's destined to displace them. Instead, we can choose to embrace Deloitte’s definition of collaborative productivity: An age of “with” that sees humans join forces with technology to tap their differing strengths, together.
For data handling, in particular, AI can act as a valuable ally. Giving employees the augmented capabilities required to address an ever-growing range of problems can empower them to tame data and use it to keep doing their jobs more effectively.

title: Council Post: The Role Of AI In Healthcare
text:
Nirav Patel is President and CEO, Bristlecone, leading the way in supply chain transformation and digital resilience.
Like every other industry, artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the landscape of healthcare and medicine. This emerging technology and its capabilities can revolutionize medicine by redefining the doctor-patient relationship and could save the healthcare industry $360 billion a year, according to McKinsey and Harvard.
In this article, I will look at how it may have more of an impact on the healthcare industry than initially meets the eye and what facets of the sector AI can revolutionize.
AI Use Cases In Healthcare
One of the major applications of AI in healthcare is when used in medical imaging and diagnostics. Algorithms are being trained on immense amounts of medical data to analyze CT scans, MRIs, X-rays, microscopy images and other medical visuals. With this training, AI can identify abnormalities, such as tumors, infections or fractures.
In some cases, these AI systems have proven more accurate than healthcare professionals in detecting anomalies when diagnosing written test cases of realistic illnesses. Likewise, Google developed a deep learning model that could detect breast cancer in mammograms that showed great accuracy and fewer false positives and negatives than human radiologists. Models like this one are trained on thousands of previous mammograms to identify telltale signs of breast cancer, including irregular shapes, sizes and edges of lesions.
This application of AI could reduce instances of misdiagnosis, whether that be false positives or negatives. Deep learning diagnostic performance models will likely quickly become an invaluable tool for healthcare professionals, assisting them in providing better patient care.
Like with applications in other industries, AI can also be used to assist human specialists with menial tasks to bolster productivity at healthcare institutions. For example, AI can help to reduce inventory losses during reconciliation. By infusing computer vision and edge devices into the reconciliation process, AI can automate the manual process of identifying and counting the inventory in a surgical tray.
AI As A Guardian
AI can also aid healthcare professionals with more than just logistics and analysis. Through wearable sensors and internet-connected devices, AI algorithms can assist in continuous remote patient monitoring.
For example, these AI systems can be invaluable in tracking health metrics and detecting any abnormal changes in real time for patients with chronic conditions like diabetes or heart disease. When the AI system detects concerning patterns, like fluctuations in heart rate or blood glucose levels, it can alert physicians or home caretakers to take preventative action.
One example of this tech is a wearable wrist sensor to monitor activity patterns and behaviors. The AI algorithm learns an individual’s habits and converts those habits to a baseline analysis and can notify caregivers if it detects falls, lack of movement or other unusual behavior that could signify emerging health problems or dangerous situations.
Similarly, diabetic patients can wear a glucose monitor linked to a smartphone app. It tracks glucose levels day and night, while the AI generates personalized insights and alerts patients when readings go above target thresholds.
Technologies enabled by AI analytics allow patients to be evaluated in their home environments instead of taking valuable space in a hospital for monitoring situations, to improve outcomes and quality of life.
What’s Next For AI In Healthcare
As healthcare enters the era of AI and more possibilities emerge, organizations everywhere should be more motivated than ever to work with healthcare providers who improve patients’ lives.
As is always the case when we stumble upon discoveries and inventions, the one thing that we must keep top of mind is how organizations can adapt and the potential for growth and change. When it comes to AI, the possibilities are seemingly endless, and this is true for the healthcare industry.
As we continue to discover what AI can do, we will of course encounter pros as well as cons, such as the missteps or stumbles that inherently come with implementing new technology or the hurdle of widespread adoption.
Privacy concerns, for example, remain top of mind, particularly in an industry that deals with such sensitive patient data. As leaders in the healthcare industry push forward into this new world, they should remain mindful of their cybersecurity, the data being used and how to maintain the crucial trust of their patients when using AI.
Though the technology may be unique, the approach to these challenges is the same as many others: purposeful steps forward, meticulous decision-making and keeping the interests of the patient in mind at all times. AI has the potential to revolutionize the healthcare industry, but rushing in without the proper knowledge or preparation will do more harm than good. Organizations should seek out the proper solutions and partners to guide this new journey.
By overcoming those challenges, AI technology offers a lot of promise for advancements in the quality of care, making life easier for patients and providers alike, and potentially reducing the cost of care significantly. Now, it’s up to those championing and developing this promising technology to plan for a bright future, and partner with those who understand the depths of AI and all that it is capable of to deliver the best results possible.

title: 5 Ways AI Can Instantly Make Your Human-To-Human Relationships More Effective
text:
There’s a lot of talk about AI being used to replace humans and potentially reduce the human-to-human relationships we enjoy in work and elsewhere. But even with these potential drawbacks, experts have also identified the potential for AI to be a source for good in human relationships — if it is used appropriately.
As it turns out, depending on how it is used, AI can actually make human-to-human relationships more effective, helping to strengthen partnerships, client relationships and more.
1. More Time To Handle Complex Needs
Chatbots are one of the most common customer-facing applications of AI, and while they are far from perfect, they can be an important difference-maker in the customer service industry. As a report from Deloitte reveals, 81% of contact centers are investing in AI tools that enable their agents to become more efficient and offer an improved customer experience.
The reason for such strong trends? AI’s ability to help customers self-service simple tasks, as well as predicting trends to improve scheduling and planning. By letting AI take care of simple requests and questions, human customer service agents had more time to address more complex issues.
Incredibly, AI is even able to help improve human interactions by analyzing the content of these conversations and presenting insights for next steps or tips for improvement. The end result is that customers with complex concerns get better, more personalized attention to resolve their issue and help them feel valued.
2. Research To Find The Right Connections
So much of the business world comes down to relationships. From business partners to the journalists you pitch public relations materials to, the right relationships can make all the difference in moving your business forward.
Of course, finding the right people to partner with, pitch and so on can become incredibly time-consuming and difficult. The American Journalist reports that there are roughly 85,000 news personnel in the United States. You don’t really have time to research and pitch them all, no matter how compelling your story might be. And generic emails aren’t likely to get you noticed.
With AI, you have a valuable tool that can help you find the right person based on their background, location, interests and other factors. Correctly identifying the right people already greatly increases your chances for success. Having extra time to devote to personalizing your pitch or presentation further increases the likelihood that they’ll want to learn more about what you have to say.
3. Improve Your Understanding Of Your Audience
Understanding your audience is a major challenge for many business leaders. After all, if you knew what did or didn’t appeal to your audience, it would be much easier to speak to them in a meaningful, engaging way that sparks lasting connections. And AI can help here, too.
This was illustrated to me during a recent conversation with James Webb, co-founder and CTO of Comb Insights, whose app uses proprietary AI to provide sentiment scores on comments on social media posts.
As he explained, “Using AI to quickly evaluate the overall sentiment of the comments on a post can give business leaders an immediate understanding of whether their content resonated with their audience. Seeing the ratio of positive to neutral or negative comments, and seeing the most common words that show up in the comments, can provide quick insights into why a post succeeded or failed.
Continued Webb, “With this instant understanding of their audience, businesses can pivot in the type of social media content they produce so they can strengthen these important digital relationships.”
4. Personalize The Customer Experience
According to a report by McKinsey, 71% of customers expect personalized interactions from the companies they do business with. This expectation can have significant consequences, with 76% of customers expressing frustration when personalization expectations aren’t met, and fast-growing companies driving a significant portion of their revenue from personalization efforts.
To deliver a personal experience, however, you must know what your audience wants and then tailor the experience to meet those desires.
AI can be a powerful tool in this regard thanks to its ability to analyze customer behaviors (such as when they visit your website), particularly by looking at activities like past purchases or customer service interactions to predict their needs and present relevant information.
When your customer service team has access to this information, they can provide the customized experience that audiences crave, strengthening relationships and fueling customer loyalty.
5. Fine-Tune Your Organization’s Voice
Your organization’s voice can go a long way in building human-to-human connections. A consistent voice on your social media posts, website and even packaging can help create a brand persona that appeals to your audience.
AI can help ensure that your organization’s voice remains consistent, regardless of who is doing the communicating. Writing for Medium, Piper Hendricks suggests using AI for Large Language Models that learn specifically from the organization’s own existing content. This can then be used to create a style guide “that ensures your team can find what they need and your final products consistently use your organizational voice.”
LLM models can then free up the creative team’s time for efforts such as personalization, while ensuring that their output still meets the organization’s style standards.
More Human Than You’d Think
As these examples reveal, AI can actually help unlock the power of our humanity more than ever. After all, there are many things that AI inherently can’t do — but there are also many things that it can do quite well. By using AI appropriately, business leaders can focus more of their efforts on strengthening the human connections that are so crucial to the success of any business endeavor.

title: Council Post: Five Emerging Trends In Pet Health Care For 2024 And Beyond
text:
Alex Douzet is CEO of Pumpkin, a pet insurance and wellness care provider founded to help ensure pets live their healthiest lives.
Pet ownership is at an all-time high, with 66% of U.S. households owning at least one pet. The global pet care market is estimated to grow from $246 billion in 2023 to $368 billion by 2030. Spending on veterinary services in the U.S. alone exceeded $38 billion in 2023, with growth in emergency care and specialty services contributing significantly.
Today's modern, multi-species family is more bonded to their pets than ever, increasing the demand for gold-standard veterinary care. As a result, we are witnessing how modern high expectations are putting pressure on veterinary clinics to provide tech-enabled conveniences.
As these cultural and economic forces converge with the rise of advanced technology and artificial intelligence, I see five key trends that will radically impact the pet health industry in 2024 and beyond.
1. Technology enablement will help bridge the veterinary supply and demand gap.
Veterinary clinics face a critical imbalance between labor supply and demand. While pet owners’ demand for veterinary care services is at an all-time high, clinics face a crippling shortage of veterinary technicians and veterinarians.
To meet demand by 2030, IDEXX estimates clinics must increase productivity by as much as 40%. To achieve this, I see telemedicine and at-home diagnostic tools, as well as strategically integrated AI, as ways to improve efficiency in delivering care.
Particularly, I see telemedicine as poised to become an essential diagnostic tool. While predominantly used for urgent care, in the future, it can allow a veterinarian to diagnose conditions and prescribe treatment remotely. This increases efficiency by allowing clinics to administer high-quality care at a faster frequency than in-clinic appointments currently allow. Likewise, the adoption of in-home diagnostic tools such as tracking collars or smart litter boxes can allow a veterinarian to monitor a pet’s health remotely, alleviating the need for frequent in-clinic exams.
2. AI tools will unlock better care outcomes and health longevity.
Sure, AI tools free up time by performing mundane tasks like managing client communications, streamlining record-keeping and summarizing medical records. However, how I see AI truly transforming the veterinary industry is in its ability to enable more accurate diagnostics and early detection of health risks. AI is paving the way for gold-standard care by allowing clinics to bring new, rapid diagnostic tests in-house so they can rely less on outsourced pathologists or lab testing.
Promising results presented at the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing showcase AI’s success in analyzing radiology results. AI can act as the veterinarian’s co-pilot, quickly and accurately analyzing diagnostic imaging and detecting abnormalities the human eye may miss. Multimodal AI tools can further assist veterinarians by synthesizing images, video and text inputs to generate a holistic summary of any health issues present.
AI’s accuracy and speed of detection are proving to be a powerful mix. I’ve observed how a veterinarian and veterinary technician using AI-powered scans were able to confirm a dog's ingestion of rat poison in minutes, radically improving their ability to quickly administer treatment.
3. Continued corporatization of vet clinics.
Today, 40% of general practices and 25% of emergency clinics are independent. In the coming years, independent clinics will likely continue to be acquired in significant numbers. The need for greater efficiency and technology investment is the driving force behind this trend.
One clinic typically doesn’t have the resources to invest in the technology needed to increase their productivity. However, when practices join a group network, optimized workflows can increase productivity and revenue, allowing them to reinvest those funds in areas that will improve the client experience such as cutting-edge medical tools and top-tier talent. I see this as vital for longevity since millennial and Gen-Z pet owners expect a frictionless client experience and the highest level of care.
4. Next-generation pet owners will drive tech-enabled convenience.
Modern pet owner have a closer relationship with their pet than previous generations. They are dedicated to giving their pets the most high-quality care, and their approach to pet care is more proactive with younger generations more likely to insure their pets: 31% of Gen-Z versus 8% of Boomers.
These generations grew up in the digital age, and their familiarity with seamless technology means they expect a digital-forward in-clinic experience. To satisfy this generation's expectations, clinics need to enable a frictionless client experience with things like digital self-check-in tools and patient intake kiosks, integrated CRM platforms spanning every visit touchpoint and better cloud-based practice management systems that consolidate client data.
5. Clinic networks may soon only accept insured pets.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index reports veterinary costs have increased by nearly 11% between July 2022 and July 2023. The sheer demand for veterinary services is straining the labor shortage, causing veterinary costs to rise at triple the rate of standard inflation, which is currently 3%.
The rising costs have made veterinary care less accessible for some pet owners, so I see the current moment as a once-in-a-lifetime growth in pet insurance uptake. In 2022, NAPHIA predicted pet insurance penetration, currently around 3%, would increase, with an overall compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16.7% between 2022 and 2030. At that rate, between a quarter and one-third of U.S. pets could be insured by 2043.
As clinics endeavor to increase productivity, they’ll likely consider the necessity of only accepting insured pets. Insured pets support costly diagnostics and treatments, so clinics know they can administer gold-standard care while remaining profitable. According to a report by Zoetis and my company, insured pets see veterinarians 1.5 times more per year compared to uninsured pets and spend almost two times more at their clinic per year.
Final Thoughts
This pivotal moment in pet health represents a unique confluence of societal and cultural shifts. In the face of transformation, it's promising to see how veterinary teams embrace emerging technology.
It's a dynamic time for this industry, with a seismic shift in human behavior, values and spending priorities that will lead to tremendous innovation in veterinary medicine and expand access to the best care possible for pets.

title: Council Post: Sustainable Banking: Charting The Future With AI And Data Analytics
text:
Senior VP and head of global consulting at ITC Infotech.
The global push for sustainability in the financial sector, driven by the need to achieve net-zero emissions, is increasing the demand for eco-friendly practices in banking. Financial institutions face growing pressure to meet stringent ESG regulations, such as the European Banking Authority's mandate for climate disclosures starting December 2023. To comply, they need to implement robust policies and procedures for risk management and regulatory reporting, necessitating the use of intelligent analytics platforms to gather and analyze ESG data.
Many financial institutions have already incorporated AI and analytics across various functions, leveraging machine learning algorithms to enhance revenue, assess credit risk, improve finance operations, and more. AI can now aid sustainable business strategies by efficiently integrating ESG considerations, offering real-time scores, transaction analysis and risk assessments for informed decision-making.
Sustainable Banking Initiatives
Enterprises that actively conceptualize and implement their sustainability agendas get a head start in the race to meet their sustainability goals. Key areas for responsible banking initiatives include:
Sustainable Products
Financial institutions have long been actively integrating sustainability principles into their business strategies, offering eco-friendly financial products, such as green car loans, green savings and bonds, green mortgages, etc. Data analytics and AI/ML can be game changers in designing a sustainable banking customer journey by enhancing existing products with sustainability features. This includes offering favorable terms for purchasing sustainable goods with credit cards, implementing mechanisms to offset carbon footprints and introducing green deposit accounts exclusively designed for sustainable investments.
Moreover, the "climate-friendly" aspect of financial enterprises is increasingly being scrutinized with the proportion of “climate-friendly loans, advances and debt securities compared to total assets" becoming a critical metric of assessment. AI-driven solutions are emerging as powerful tools to assist investors in evaluating companies' financial prospects alongside ESG (environmental, social and governance) factors.
Matthew Slovik, head of global sustainable finance at Morgan Stanley, highlights the significance of this integration: “The integration of AI into sustainable investing could mark a profound turning point in investors’ ability to navigate the complex web of ESG factors. By harnessing AI’s analytical capabilities, investors can identify companies with strong ESG performance, mitigate risks, and shape portfolios that better align with sustainability objectives.”
Supply Chain Ecosystems
For a supply chain to be sustainable, it's essential to have a strong and effective rating system that prioritizes organizations that adhere to certain sustainability standards. Advanced analytics is required for assessing and managing ESG risk across the network.
For example, enterprises can evaluate the volume and categories of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions contributed by each supplier to the aggregate supply chain emissions and set policies outlining minimum standards. Numerous leading international banks—such as Citi Bank, Bank of America, DBS, Deutsche Bank and others—are actively engaged in sustainable procurement practices. These practices aim to minimize waste, support fair working conditions and contribute to economic growth. Moreover, banks are increasingly channeling significant funds into third-party vendors, mandating vendor sustainability as a key criterion to enhance ESG accountability and transparency throughout the supply chain.
Regulatory Compliance And ESG Assessment
Implementation of ESG in banking demands advanced technology and a nuanced understanding of crucial data points for present and future ESG metrics. Though there is an abundance of data, it is not standardized, making comparisons difficult, diminishing reliability and value. Gen AI solutions can automate data harvesting, organize dictionaries and metadata from internal IT systems and map them to an ESG data model. AI is particularly helpful in uncovering information from siloed IT systems and various unstructured formats.
The Challenges To The Sustainability Initiative
Measuring Sustainability ne of the key challenges in measuring sustainability is the lack of a uniform industry framework. Existing frameworks like BEI (business environment index) and TCFD (task force on climate-related financial disclosures) are not universally adopted.
Unlike financial reporting with predefined parameters like assets, liabilities, net profit or EBITDA, ESG reporting lacks a uniform mechanism. The absence of such standards creates variability in approaches across the banking sector. Ongoing efforts by industry consortiums aim to establish standardized procedures for ESG evaluation, promoting a more consistent approach industry-wide.
Data Collection And Management
Financial institutions typically obtain ESG data from open channels, company disclosures or external providers. Gen AI can compile this data from various sources to construct a reliable database for subsequent analysis. However, scaling up requires adaptation of IT systems to systematically collect, aggregate and report a broad range of sustainability data. Many of the institutions lack a comprehensive approach to integrate sustainability data into existing reporting and act on sustainability KPIs and KRIs.
Concerns About AI
AI in ESG assessment, while powerful, raises privacy concerns due to extensive data collection. Risks include the potential lack of reliability and accountability in AI-generated information, with the possibility of biases—algorithmic or human—seeping in without safeguards for transparency and accountability. Despite these concerns, AI's learning and adaptive capabilities improve over time, resulting in better accuracy.
Conclusion
Sustainability and AI are two key trends shaping the future of financial services. Driven by ESG regulations, financial institutions are adopting intelligent analytics platforms guided by technology, data and talent. While challenges exist in data collection and measurement, addressing them requires a multidisciplinary approach, involving technological advancements, regulatory compliance, and a shift toward more systematic and integrated frameworks for sustainability reporting and assessment.
As the financial sector navigates these challenges, AI and data analytics emerge as both a solution and a pivotal force, propelling the industry toward a more sustainable, accountable and innovative future.

title: Deloitte BrandVoice: Inspiring Employees To Trust The Coming GenAI-Fueled Workplace
text:
Like the invention of steam and electric power, or digital-age milestones such as the internet and smart phones, the arrival of Generative AI (GenAI) feels like one of those seismic moments in which business, work, and society are forever changed.
Just as the original industrial revolution was met with resistance, the advent of GenAI is not universally welcomed. GenAI-enabled tools are a long way from the machinery that transformed work in the 19th century, but the concern is similar: machines threatening to replace humans. Clearly, one of the first major tests GenAI needs to pass is one of trust. Although global business leaders who responded to a new Deloitte AI Institute survey overwhelmingly believe it will positively transform their organization, just over half of them also believe it will centralize power and increase economic inequality.
GenAI holds immense potential in the productivity gains and differentiation it can deliver. But before that can happen, I believe that leaders will need to diligently tackle the issue of trust. This is because the people that hold many of the keys to an organization’s success—the employees—arguably have the most at stake when introducing GenAI into the workplace.
Since many of us derive a great deal of our sense of identity and self-worth from work, the prospect of GenAI taking over even a small proportion of that work has the potential to affect morale and productivity. One study predicts that two-thirds of current jobs in the US and Europe will be exposed to some degree of AI automation, and it’s likely to affect women more, with some 80% of women in professions likely to be most affected by GenAI (compared to 60% of men).
It is not a matter that leaders can afford to ignore.
Across industries and sectors, executives are currently focused on the big question of where and how to start implementing GenAI. I believe it is equally important that they start thinking about how to “future-proof” their workforce for the GenAI age. It’s not just a question of gaining the acceptance of employees on the GenAI journey—it’s about engaging them to help reshape the organization for a new era of work in which GenAI empowers humans to operate in new dimensions of innovation and productivity. Bringing employees along the organization’s AI journey encourages them to work with AI rather than around it. In this new digital workforce, GenAI will not just be about automating repetitive tasks, but unleashing the extraordinary potential between human and artificial intelligence—and along with it, the possibilities to discover new ideas, products, services and completely new kinds of jobs.
How do we get there? World leaders are debating that topic now at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting (Davos) with this year’s theme being ‘Rebuilding Trust.’ I agree that it’s important for leaders to start laying the groundwork now, and I believe these are crucial steps:
- The first step is to ensure that everyone in the organization who will likely be affected by GenAI has an opportunity to shape the discussion. This involves maintaining transparency into the AI business strategy and work; to create a fuller understanding of machines’ growing role in the workplace, the integral role that humans play, and a more successful transformation.
- Workforce input is even more vital given the trust and ethical issues that accompany AI. Diversity of cultural, gender, and social viewpoints, and clear governance and guidelines, are crucial factors in the complex equations that go into formulating GenAI solutions that are fair and trustworthy for the users as well as end customers.
- We are naturally inclined to fear things we don’t understand. Therefore, a key component of workplace AI strategy will need to be education, with learning and reskilling programs as the cornerstone of turning apprehension into acceptance, fluency and enthusiasm. (Notably, only 47% of respondents in Deloitte’s The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise survey believe they are doing enough to educate employees on AI’s benefits). At Deloitte, we are helping infuse the new technology into our work with an “AI Fluency” initiative to provide our people with a range of learning tools on everything from basic GenAI prompt usage to deeper dives into AI components such as natural language processing.
These steps are table stakes for organizations looking to manage the advent of GenAI into their workforce. But if I had to single out one success factor, it would be communication. There are many game-changing technologies, such as the cloud, metaverse, and edge computing, that can bring businesses enduring value and create new markets; but there is probably only one that requires them to rethink the very nature of work in the future, and that is GenAI. Effective communication from the C-suite, enabled by human capital teams, can make the difference between painful upheaval and positive transformation.
It is up to leaders to articulate transparently to managers and employees at all levels their vision for GenAI and their expectations of what it will mean. If they can communicate the advantages of the “human with machines” workplace and do it in a way that inspires trust and alignment, I think they will be laying a solid path to success.

title: Council Post: When AI Meets Infrastructure: Top Considerations For IT Leaders
text:
Mark Mahle is CEO of NetActuate.
We are in the midst of a seismic shift in the technology landscape. Artificial intelligence is transforming industries and redefining the boundaries of what is possible.
In McKinsey’s list of top eight priorities for CEOs in 2024, No. 1 is generative AI and No. 2 is outcompeting with technology. Forrester founder and CEO George Colony called generative AI "the most important technology thunderstorm of the last 40 years,” and the company’s September 2023 AI survey found that 62% of companies are either experimenting with (29%) or expanding (33%) GenAI.
New AI applications are emerging at breakneck speed, a reality that is both thrilling and daunting. I feel as though we’re at the beginning of a gold rush, where we need to temper our ambition with caution. The bottom line is that AI apps are incredibly resource-intensive, requiring unprecedented levels of processing power, GPU usage, bandwidth and storage.
I see business leaders getting caught up in the excitement of AI’s possibilities and immediately wanting to integrate AI into their existing tools or building AI apps from scratch. But deploying AI involves complex factors that can rapidly deplete thousands or millions of dollars in a company’s budget. I love embracing new technologies and helping clients implement them for their benefit—but I think it’s crucial for IT leaders to take a step back and evaluate all of the implications before jumping headfirst into an AI investment. Here are four key elements I recommend taking into consideration.
1. AI And Processing Power
AI applications offer impressive performance but have significant processing requirements. For example, a single server containing AI chips may use twice as much power as an entire rack of 40 servers.
The GPUs needed to run AI efficiently can be much more expensive than other types of apps without AI features. Shortages can also be an issue, since demand is sky-high right now, so plan ahead. Think carefully about whether owning equipment or using public cloud resources makes more sense from a cost perspective. It can be pricey to constantly upgrade your hardware, but so can burning through resources from a public cloud provider. Look at all options, and weigh them carefully before making a decision.
2. AI Impact On Data Centers
AI’s massive energy requirements are increasing the already hefty burden on data centers in today’s landscape of online services. Today, data centers account for around 1% to 1.5% of global energy use, but a recent analysis estimated that, if current AI trends continue, NVIDIA will ship 1.5 million AI server units per year by 2027. These servers could consume approximately 85.4 terawatt-hours of electricity each year, surpassing the energy use of many small countries.
Unless you are running your apps on premises, you will use data centers to run your AI servers and storage. These data centers are likely to consume significant amounts of energy to process, cool and maintain this extremely high-performance infrastructure. You can do much more with AI than with other technologies, but AI apps have high capital and operating costs. Run the actual numbers, and weigh the costs and benefits of AI apps.
Look at the small details that can have a big impact over time. For example, is physical proximity important for the information you need to process? If using a data center 100 miles away versus 10 miles away costs an extra penny per transaction, at scale, that difference could translate to millions of dollars. How can you build efficiencies into apps so they are less resource-intensive? If you are running apps on your own equipment, ask potential providers about their power and cooling capacity and plans for future usage. Consider diversifying your providers to ensure redundancy and mitigate risks in case of disaster.
3. AI At The Edge
AI applications need to be delivered at the edge, as close as possible to the edge of the network and to users, devices and data sources. The types of apps that should be at the edge are those that you want people to interact with as quickly as possible, such as conversational GenAI apps or other real-time services, alerts and scans.
Latency is a major consideration in ensuring these apps perform seamlessly. How can you manage load balancing to distribute traffic effectively? What technology can you use to give end users access to the nearest application resource node and ensure there are enough proximal nodes to handle all incoming requests?
4. Ensemble AI
Not all AI is created equal, whether you are building and deploying apps in house or working with third-party partners. It’s important to evaluate not just the resources needed to develop an AI app but also the infrastructure and network that it needs to run on. Consider a modular approach to AI at the edge, using ensemble AI, composed of multiple smaller AI engines that each have specific tasks and work intelligently together. Ensemble AI allows you to prioritize your own use cases for business or technology reasons and pass through additional functionality to other AI apps, inside or outside your stack.
AI is bound to shape the future of business and technology. It can open up extraordinary possibilities for your business, but it can also drain your resources at lightning speed. Take a measured, clear-eyed approach to investing in AI. Analyze the risks and rewards, costs and benefits—and make an informed decision about your next steps.
